questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASC 305, an investment qualifies as a cash equivalent when it is

answers.text: A short-term, highly liquid investment readily convertible to a known cash amount with an original maturity of three months or less from the date of purchase — presenting insignificant risk of value changes
Any investment held in a money market account, regardless of maturity or withdrawal restrictions
Any debt security with remaining maturity of three months or less at the balance sheet date, regardless of when purchased
Any short-term available-for-sale security with fair value close to amortized cost

explanations.a: ASC 305-10-20 defines cash equivalents as short-term, highly liquid investments that are (1) readily convertible to known amounts of cash and (2) so near their maturity that they present insignificant risk of value changes. The operative criterion is an original maturity of three months or less from the date of purchase. Examples include 90-day Treasury bills, commercial paper with ≤90-day maturities, and qualifying money market funds.
explanations.b: Not all money market accounts qualify — some have withdrawal restrictions or invest in instruments with maturities exceeding three months. The original maturity criterion must be satisfied independently of the account type.
explanations.c: The classification is based on original maturity from the purchase date — not remaining maturity at the balance sheet date. A 6-month T-bill purchased 5 months ago does NOT qualify as a cash equivalent because its original maturity exceeded 3 months.
explanations.d: Available-for-sale classification applies to debt and equity securities under ASC 320. Instruments meeting the cash equivalent definition are excluded from ASC 320 scope and presented in Cash and Cash Equivalents.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: On December 1, a company purchases a 60-day commercial paper instrument with face value of $500,000. How should this investment be classified on the December 31 balance sheet?

answers.text: Short-term investment — commercial paper is never classified as a cash equivalent
Long-term investment — all commercial paper is a long-term holding
Cash equivalent — the 60-day original maturity at purchase is within the three-month threshold, qualifying it as a cash equivalent
Trading security — all short-term debt instruments are classified as trading securities under ASC 320

explanations.a: Commercial paper with an original maturity of 60 days does qualify as a cash equivalent under ASC 305. The instrument type does not disqualify it — the original maturity is what matters.
explanations.b: A 60-day commercial paper is short-term by nature and qualifies as a cash equivalent — not a long-term investment.
explanations.c: The 60-day original maturity from the purchase date (December 1) falls within the 3-month (~90-day) threshold. The instrument is (1) short-term and highly liquid; (2) readily convertible to a known cash amount; and (3) purchased with original maturity ≤3 months — satisfying the ASC 305 cash equivalent definition. Classification is determined at purchase and does not change as the instrument approaches maturity.
explanations.d: Cash equivalents are specifically excluded from ASC 320. They are presented in the Cash and Cash Equivalents line item, not as investment securities.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A bond indenture requires maintaining $2 million in a segregated sinking fund for bond repayment in four years. How should this $2 million be classified on the balance sheet?

answers.text: Cash and Cash Equivalents — all cash held by the entity belongs in this line item
Current asset — the sinking fund will ultimately repay a long-term obligation
Operating cash reserve — bond-related cash is an operating asset
Non-current restricted asset labeled 'Restricted Cash' or 'Sinking Fund' — legally restricted from general use with restriction extending beyond one year

explanations.a: Legally restricted cash cannot be included in Cash and Cash Equivalents — doing so overstates available liquidity. ASC 305-10-45 requires restricted cash to be presented separately.
explanations.b: The bonds mature in four years — the restriction lifts only then. Since the restriction extends beyond one year, the sinking fund is a non-current, not current, asset.
explanations.c: 'Operating cash reserve' is not a defined US GAAP balance sheet category. Legally restricted non-current cash is a non-current restricted asset.
explanations.d: ASC 305-10-45 requires that legally restricted cash (such as bond indenture sinking funds) be excluded from Cash and Cash Equivalents and presented separately. Since the bonds mature in four years, the sinking fund is a non-current restricted asset labeled accordingly ('Sinking Fund' or 'Restricted Cash, non-current') to communicate to users that this cash is unavailable for general operations.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company's Bank A checking account has a positive balance of $80,000; its Bank B account has a $25,000 overdraft. No legal right of offset exists between the two banks. How are these amounts presented on the balance sheet?

answers.text: $80,000 in Cash and Cash Equivalents; $25,000 as a current liability (Bank Overdraft) — no right of offset between different banks means they cannot be netted
$55,000 net in Cash and Cash Equivalents — all bank balances are netted together
$80,000 in Cash and Cash Equivalents; the overdraft is disclosed only in footnotes
Both accounts excluded from the balance sheet pending resolution of the overdraft

explanations.a: When an overdraft exists at a different bank from positive balances, and no right of offset exists, the amounts cannot be netted. Bank A positive balance ($80,000) is in Cash and Cash Equivalents; Bank B overdraft ($25,000) is a current liability. If both were at the same bank with a legal right of offset, netting would be permissible.
explanations.b: Netting requires a legally enforceable right of offset plus intent to settle net (ASC 210-20). Without such a right, netting is prohibited regardless of the entity's preferences.
explanations.c: Bank overdrafts are actual liabilities that must appear on the face of the balance sheet — not merely in footnotes. A $25,000 overdraft is a real obligation to the bank.
explanations.d: Both amounts require balance sheet presentation; overdraft status does not remove items from recognition.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASU 2016-18, how must restricted cash be reflected in the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: Restricted cash is included with unrestricted cash and cash equivalents in both the beginning-of-period and end-of-period totals — changes in restricted cash are not separately classified as operating, investing, or financing activities
Changes in restricted cash are classified as investing activities
Restricted cash is excluded from the statement of cash flows and disclosed only in footnotes
Changes in restricted cash are classified as financing activities

explanations.a: ASU 2016-18 amended ASC 230 to require that the statement of cash flows explain the change in the total of cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash. The beginning and ending balance reconciliation must include all restricted cash amounts. A supplemental reconciliation to balance sheet line items is required. This eliminated the prior practice of classifying transfers between unrestricted and restricted accounts as investing activities — which showed apparent cash flows without real external cash receipts or payments.
explanations.b: ASU 2016-18 specifically eliminated classifying transfers between unrestricted and restricted cash as investing activities. Restricted cash is now part of the overall beginning and ending totals.
explanations.c: Restricted cash affects the beginning and ending balances in the statement of cash flows — it is not excluded. Note disclosure is also required, but the primary change was to include restricted cash in the statement's reconciliation amounts.
explanations.d: Restricted cash is not classified as financing activities. Under ASU 2016-18 it is included in the cash balance totals rather than classified into any activity section.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: On November 1, a company invests $1,000,000 in a 180-day Certificate of Deposit. At December 31, 61 days remain until maturity. How should this CD be classified, and why?

answers.text: Cash equivalent — only 61 days remain at year-end, within the 3-month threshold
Long-term investment — CDs are always classified as long-term
Short-term investment — the CD was purchased with a 180-day original maturity exceeding 3 months; it does not qualify as a cash equivalent regardless of remaining days at year-end
Cash equivalent — CDs with fewer than 90 days remaining at the balance sheet date always qualify

explanations.a: Remaining maturity at the balance sheet date does not determine cash equivalent classification. The original maturity at the purchase date is the operative criterion.
explanations.b: A 180-day CD matures within one year and is a short-term investment (current asset) — not a long-term investment.
explanations.c: ASC 305-10-20 defines the 3-month threshold based on original maturity from the date of purchase. This CD was purchased November 1 with a 180-day original maturity — exceeding 3 months. Therefore, it does not qualify as a cash equivalent at any point during its life. At December 31, it is classified as a short-term investment (current asset).
explanations.d: A '90-days-remaining' test does not exist in US GAAP. The original maturity from the purchase date is the sole criterion. A CD purchased with a 180-day term remains a short-term investment throughout — it is never reclassified as a cash equivalent.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company maintains a $400,000 compensating balance under a legally binding deposit agreement expiring in 20 months, and an informal 'goodwill' balance of $60,000 that the bank requests but cannot legally enforce. How should each amount be classified?

answers.text: Both amounts ($460,000 total) classified as restricted cash — all maintained bank balances are compensating balances
Both amounts included in Cash and Cash Equivalents — compensating balances require only footnote disclosure, not reclassification
Both excluded from Cash and Cash Equivalents and classified as non-current restricted assets

The $400,000 formal compensating balance: non-current restricted cash (restriction extends 20 months); the $60,000 informal goodwill balance: remains in Cash and Cash Equivalents since it is not legally restricted

explanations.a: Informally maintained goodwill balances that are not legally enforceable are not restricted and remain in Cash and Cash Equivalents. Only legally binding restrictions create compensating balances requiring reclassification.
explanations.b: Formally required (legally binding) compensating balances must be excluded from Cash and Cash Equivalents and separately classified — footnote disclosure is in addition to, not instead of, proper classification.
explanations.c: The informal goodwill balance is not legally restricted — it is available for use. Only the formal legally binding balance is excluded.
explanations.d: ASC 305-10-50 distinguishes formal from informal compensating balances: (1) Formal — legally binding agreements restrict use. The $400,000 cannot be used for other purposes; the 20-month duration makes it a non-current restricted asset; (2) Informal — merely requested by the bank without legal enforcement. The $60,000 remains at the company's full disposal and stays in Cash and Cash Equivalents. Footnote disclosure of both arrangements is required.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company has $1,200,000 of restricted cash classified as non-current under a bond indenture sinking fund. The bonds now have only 9 months remaining until maturity. On the December 31 balance sheet, how should this restricted cash be classified?

answers.text: Non-current — sinking funds remain non-current until bonds actually mature and are repaid
Written off — sinking funds are not recognized as assets near maturity
Cash and Cash Equivalents — the 9-month remaining term effectively makes the restriction short-term

Current restricted cash — the restriction expires within 12 months (bonds mature in 9 months), requiring reclassification from non-current to current; it is not yet unrestricted Cash and Cash Equivalents since the legal restriction has not lifted

explanations.a: Current/non-current classification follows the expected time until the restriction expires. When expiration falls within 12 months, reclassification from non-current to current is required — consistent with the general principle that items expected to be realized within one year are current.
explanations.b: Sinking fund cash is a real asset — it will be applied to bond repayment at maturity.
explanations.c: Restricted cash does not become unrestricted Cash and Cash Equivalents as the restriction's expiration approaches — the legal restriction persists until the bonds mature. The reclassification moves it from non-current to current restricted cash only.
explanations.d: The bonds mature in 9 months — within one year. The sinking fund restriction will therefore expire in 9 months, after which the cash becomes available. This triggers reclassification from non-current to current restricted cash on the December 31 balance sheet. It remains labeled as restricted (e.g., 'Current Restricted Cash — Bond Sinking Fund') rather than unrestricted Cash and Cash Equivalents because the legal restriction has not yet lifted. When the bonds mature and are repaid, the cash is released from restriction.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: The allowance for doubtful accounts is classified on the balance sheet as

answers.text: A current liability — amounts potentially owed customers for credit adjustments
A stockholders' equity account — retained earnings set aside for bad debt losses
A contra-asset account that reduces gross accounts receivable to net realizable value — the amount the company estimates will actually be collected
A non-current asset — representing the long-term collectability reserve

explanations.a: The allowance is not a liability — it is a contra-asset representing management's estimate of uncollectible receivables, with no obligation to customers.
explanations.b: The allowance is not a stockholders' equity component. It is a balance sheet contra-asset deducted from gross accounts receivable.
explanations.c: The allowance for doubtful accounts has a normal credit balance and is presented as a deduction from gross accounts receivable. The result — net accounts receivable — represents the net realizable value: the amount management estimates will be collected. ASC 310 requires reporting receivables at their net realizable value.
explanations.d: Accounts receivable and the related allowance are current assets. The allowance is a contra to current accounts receivable — not a non-current reserve.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A specific customer's $8,000 account is determined uncollectible and written off under the allowance method. What is the effect on net income and net accounts receivable?

answers.text: Net income decreases $8,000; net accounts receivable decreases $8,000 — the write-off triggers bad debt expense
No effect on net income; no effect on net accounts receivable — both gross AR and the allowance decrease by $8,000, leaving net AR unchanged; bad debt expense was recognized in a prior period
Net income increases $8,000 — writing off uncollectible amounts reduces future obligations
Net income decreases $8,000; net accounts receivable is unchanged — expense recognized but net receivables stay the same

explanations.a: Under the allowance method, no bad debt expense is recognized at write-off — that expense was recognized in a prior period when the allowance was created. The write-off is not an income statement event.
explanations.b: Write-off journal entry: Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $8,000 / Credit Accounts Receivable $8,000. Effect: Gross AR decreases $8,000; allowance (contra-asset) decreases $8,000; net AR = gross AR - allowance is unchanged; no expense recognized = no net income effect. The write-off removes a specific account that was already anticipated as uncollectible when the allowance was established.
explanations.c: Writing off an account does not increase net income — no credit is made to a revenue or income account.
explanations.d: Net income is not affected at write-off under the allowance method. Bad debt expense was recognized in a prior period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Using the percentage of accounts receivable (balance sheet) method, the aging analysis indicates the allowance should have a $45,000 ending balance. Before adjustment, the allowance has a $5,000 debit balance from prior write-offs exceeding the prior allowance. What is bad debt expense?

answers.text: $40,000 — adjusted from the current balance to the $45,000 target
$45,000 — the target balance equals bad debt expense under the balance sheet method
$5,000 — only the debit balance is recognized as expense
$50,000 — the entry must convert a $5,000 debit balance to a $45,000 credit balance, requiring a $50,000 credit to the allowance and corresponding debit to expense

explanations.a: This calculation applies if the allowance had a $5,000 credit balance — only $40,000 more would be needed. With a $5,000 debit balance, more is needed to first eliminate the debit before creating the credit target.
explanations.b: The bad debt expense equals the incremental adjustment needed, not always the target balance. When the allowance has an existing balance, expense is the amount to reach the target.
explanations.c: $5,000 covers only eliminating the debit balance — it would leave the allowance at zero, far short of the $45,000 required.
explanations.d: A debit balance in the allowance means write-offs exceeded prior estimates, leaving the allowance on the wrong side. To reach a $45,000 credit target: (1) eliminate the $5,000 debit balance = $5,000 credit; (2) create the $45,000 credit target = $45,000 more credit. Total credit to Allowance = $50,000. Bad Debt Expense = $50,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A previously written-off customer account of $4,000 is unexpectedly recovered in full. What journal entries are required?

answers.text: Single entry: Debit Cash $4,000 / Credit Bad Debt Recovery Revenue $4,000
Two entries: (1) Debit Accounts Receivable $4,000 / Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $4,000; then (2) Debit Cash $4,000 / Credit Accounts Receivable $4,000
Single entry: Debit Cash $4,000 / Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $4,000
Single entry: Debit Accounts Receivable $4,000 / Credit Bad Debt Expense $4,000

explanations.a: Crediting a recovery revenue account bypasses reinstatement of the accounts receivable — losing the customer's payment history.
explanations.b: Standard two-entry recovery procedure: (1) Reinstate the receivable — reverse the write-off: Debit AR $4,000 / Credit Allowance $4,000; (2) Record cash receipt: Debit Cash $4,000 / Credit AR $4,000. Net effect: Cash up $4,000; gross AR unchanged; allowance up $4,000; net AR unchanged; no income statement effect. Reinstating the account preserves important credit history for future credit decisions.
explanations.c: Bypassing the AR reinstatement produces the same balance sheet result mechanically but loses the customer payment history and creates an incomplete audit trail.
explanations.d: This is an incomplete entry — it reinstates the receivable but doesn't record the cash collection. The two-step process must be completed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company sells $500,000 of accounts receivable to a factor without recourse (factor assumes all credit risk). The factor charges a 3% fee ($15,000). What is the accounting treatment?

answers.text: Receivables remain on the balance sheet — without-recourse sales are always secured borrowings
No loss recognized — without-recourse factoring transfers all risk so the company receives full proceeds
Receivables removed from the balance sheet; cash of $485,000 recorded; loss on sale of $15,000 recognized — the factoring fee is the cost of converting receivables to immediate cash
The $15,000 fee is recorded as interest expense — factoring costs are financing charges

explanations.a: Without-recourse factoring that meets ASC 860's derecognition criteria is a true sale — not a secured borrowing. The absence of recourse satisfies the isolation criterion.
explanations.b: The company does not receive the full $500,000 — the factor deducts a 3% fee ($15,000) for assuming credit risk. Cash received = $485,000.
explanations.c: Under ASC 860-10-40, when the three derecognition criteria are met: (1) remove $500,000 AR from balance sheet; (2) record $485,000 cash received; (3) recognize $15,000 loss on sale. The loss reflects the cost of immediate liquidity by transferring credit risk to the factor.
explanations.d: The factoring fee is a loss on sale (or factoring expense) — not interest expense. It compensates the factor for credit risk assumption and collection services, not for lending money.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under the CECL model (ASU 2016-13, ASC 326), how does credit loss recognition for trade receivables differ from the prior incurred loss model?

answers.text: CECL recognizes losses only after a specific account becomes uncollectible — stricter evidence requirements than before

Under CECL, lifetime expected credit losses are recognized on Day 1 of the receivable's life — no trigger event required; the allowance reflects historical experience, current conditions, and reasonable forward-looking forecasts
CECL applies only to long-term financial instruments — trade receivables continue under the incurred loss model
CECL replaces judgment-based estimates with a fixed 2% allowance rate applied to all outstanding receivables

explanations.a: CECL requires earlier recognition — not later. The prior incurred loss model required a triggering event (evidence of probable loss) before recognition. CECL eliminates the trigger requirement.
explanations.b: ASU 2016-13 replaced the incurred loss model with CECL. Under the prior model, an objective trigger event had to occur before a credit loss could be recognized. CECL requires Day 1 recognition of all expected credit losses over the life of the receivable, using: (1) historical loss rates by cohort; (2) current economic conditions adjustment; (3) reasonable and supportable forward-looking information. This produces larger, earlier allowances that reduce net receivables from the moment of origination.
explanations.c: ASU 2016-13 explicitly covers trade receivables and contract assets — it is not limited to long-term instruments.
explanations.d: CECL requires entity-specific judgment-based estimates — no fixed rate replaces professional judgment.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: The allowance for doubtful accounts has a pre-adjustment credit balance of $60,000. The aging analysis indicates the required balance is $75,000. No write-offs or recoveries occurred during the year. What is bad debt expense, and how does the adjustment affect net accounts receivable?

answers.text: Bad debt expense = $15,000; allowance increases to $75,000; net AR decreases by $15,000
Bad debt expense = $75,000; allowance becomes $135,000; net AR decreases by $75,000
Bad debt expense = $75,000; allowance increases to $75,000 (existing balance ignored)
No adjustment needed — the existing $60,000 approximates the required amount

explanations.a: Under the balance sheet (aging) method, the adjusting entry brings the allowance to the target balance. Since allowance already has $60,000 credit and target is $75,000, only $15,000 additional credit needed. Journal entry: Debit Bad Debt Expense $15,000 / Credit Allowance $15,000. Effect: Allowance increases from $60,000 to $75,000; net AR decreases by $15,000; cash is unaffected.
explanations.b: Adding $75,000 to the existing $60,000 produces a $135,000 allowance — overstating expected losses. The balance sheet method adjusts to the target, not adds the target to the existing balance.
explanations.c: Bad debt expense equals the incremental adjustment ($15,000) — not the full target balance. The existing $60,000 must be acknowledged.
explanations.d: The $60,000 allowance is $15,000 short of the required $75,000. GAAP requires adjusting to management's best estimate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Company A factors $1,000,000 of accounts receivable with recourse (factor may require repurchase of uncollected balances). The factor charges a 4% fee ($40,000). The recourse obligation has a fair value of $25,000. Assuming the ASC 860 sale criteria are met, what total loss does Company A recognize?

answers.text: $40,000 — only the factoring fee is the loss
$65,000 — factoring fee ($40,000) plus fair value of recourse obligation ($25,000)
$0 — with-recourse factoring never produces a loss since recourse protects the factor
$25,000 — only the recourse obligation is recognized; the fee is interest expense

explanations.a: The factoring fee is part of the loss calculation, but the recourse obligation must also be recognized — omitting the $25,000 understates the total economic cost.
explanations.b: When the ASC 860 sale criteria are met: Proceeds received = $1,000,000 × 96% = $960,000. Recourse liability recognized at FV = $25,000. Loss = Book value ($1,000,000) − Proceeds ($960,000) + Recourse obligation FV ($25,000) = $65,000. Journal: Debit Cash $960,000; Debit Loss on Sale $65,000; Credit Recourse Liability $25,000; Credit AR $1,000,000. The $65,000 loss captures both the factoring discount and the obligation assumed.
explanations.c: With-recourse factoring produces a loss incorporating both the fee and the recourse obligation fair value.
explanations.d: The factoring fee is a component of the total loss on sale — not interest expense. Both the fee and the recourse obligation fair value combine in the loss calculation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: In a period of consistently rising prices, which inventory cost flow assumption produces the LOWEST ending inventory and HIGHEST cost of goods sold?

answers.text: FIFO — assigns oldest (lowest) costs to COGS
LIFO — assigns most recent (highest) costs to COGS, leaving oldest (lowest) costs in ending inventory
Weighted average — produces middle values for both COGS and ending inventory
Specific identification — results vary based on which specific items were actually sold

explanations.a: FIFO produces the HIGHEST ending inventory (most recent, higher-cost units remain) and LOWEST COGS (older, cheaper costs flow to COGS first) in a rising-price environment.
explanations.b: Under LIFO in rising prices: the most recent (highest cost) inventory is assumed sold first, producing the HIGHEST COGS and LOWEST ending inventory (consisting of oldest, cheapest layers). This reduces taxable income — a primary reason companies adopt LIFO — and creates a growing LIFO reserve over time.
explanations.c: Weighted average produces intermediate results between FIFO and LIFO.
explanations.d: Specific identification depends on which specific units were sold — no consistent directional relationship with price trends.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company uses the periodic weighted-average cost method. Beginning inventory: 100 units at $10. Purchases: 400 units at $12. Units sold: 350. What is the weighted-average unit cost and ending inventory value?

answers.text: Weighted-average cost = $10.00; ending inventory = $1,500
Weighted-average cost = $12.00; ending inventory = $1,800
Weighted-average cost = $11.00; ending inventory = $1,650
Weighted-average cost = $11.60; ending inventory (150 units) = $1,740

explanations.a: $10.00 is only the beginning inventory unit cost — not the weighted average blending all units and costs.
explanations.b: $12.00 is only the purchase cost — not the weighted average incorporating the lower-cost beginning inventory.
explanations.c: $11.00 is a simple (unweighted) average of $10 and $12 — not the quantity-weighted average.
explanations.d: Weighted-average cost = Total cost available / Total units available. Total cost = (100 × $10) + (400 × $12) = $1,000 + $4,800 = $5,800. Total units = 500. Weighted-average = $5,800 / 500 = $11.60. Ending units = 500 − 350 = 150. Ending inventory = 150 × $11.60 = $1,740. COGS = 350 × $11.60 = $4,060. Check: $1,740 + $4,060 = $5,800 ✓.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Inventory costing $70,000 has a net realizable value (NRV) of $62,000. The company uses FIFO. Under ASC 330 (as amended by ASU 2015-11), how is this inventory reported?

answers.text: Reported at $62,000 (NRV); $8,000 write-down recognized as a loss in cost of goods sold
Reported at $70,000 — write-downs are required only when NRV reaches zero
Reported at $62,000; the $8,000 is credited to OCI — inventory losses bypass the income statement
Write-down required only if management believes the decline is permanent

explanations.a: ASU 2015-11 simplified inventory measurement for FIFO and weighted-average users: inventory is measured at lower of cost or net realizable value (LCNRV). NRV = estimated selling price less costs of completion and selling. Since NRV ($62,000) < cost ($70,000), the inventory must be written down to $62,000. The $8,000 write-down is recognized in the income statement — in COGS or separately if material. Once written down, the new basis is $62,000; subsequent write-ups above this level are prohibited.
explanations.b: Write-down to NRV is required for any decline below cost — no threshold requiring NRV to reach zero.
explanations.c: Inventory write-downs reduce net income — they are not OCI items.
explanations.d: The temporary vs. permanent distinction applies to certain investments (e.g., equity securities) — not to inventory under ASC 330. All NRV declines below cost require write-down.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A retailer ships 500 units to a dealer on consignment. The dealer sells goods on the retailer's behalf. At year-end, 200 units have been sold; 300 units remain with the dealer. How should the 300 unsold units be reported?

answers.text: Not reported by the retailer — once shipped, inventory is removed from the retailer's books regardless of consignment terms
Reported in the dealer's (consignee's) inventory — goods are physically at the dealer's location
Reported in the retailer's (consignor's) inventory at cost — consignment goods remain the consignor's property until sold to an end customer; the consignee holds them as a custodian
Split between the retailer and dealer based on the commission percentage

explanations.a: Consignment shipments do not transfer title — the consignor retains legal ownership until the consignee sells goods to an end customer. Physical delivery is not a sale.
explanations.b: Consignees do not include consignment inventory in their own inventory — they hold the goods as custodians. The consignee records no inventory asset and recognizes only commission revenue upon sale.
explanations.c: The 300 unsold units are still owned by the retailer (consignor) and must be included in the retailer's inventory at cost. Only when the consignee sells goods to an end customer does the retailer recognize revenue and remove those units from inventory. Physical location does not determine accounting ownership for consignment goods.
explanations.d: Inventory ownership is not split based on commission arrangements. All 300 units belong entirely to the consignor until sold.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A LIFO company experiences a LIFO liquidation — ending inventory quantities are below beginning levels, dipping into old LIFO layers at $8 per unit while current replacement cost is $15 per unit. How does LIFO liquidation affect reported income?

answers.text: LIFO liquidation decreases reported income — older LIFO layers carry higher historical costs than current prices
LIFO liquidation increases reported income because old low-cost LIFO layers charged to COGS at $8 produce lower COGS (and higher gross profit) than charging current $15 replacement cost
LIFO liquidation has no income effect — only inventory quantities change, not costs
LIFO liquidation decreases both income and inventory — the liquidation creates a loss

explanations.a: In a rising-price environment, older LIFO layers carry LOWER costs — not higher. When liquidated, these cheap historical-cost layers produce lower COGS and higher income.
explanations.b: LIFO liquidation produces 'inventory profits' when older, cheaper layers flow to COGS. Here the old layer at $8 goes to COGS vs. $15 replacement cost — COGS is $7 per unit lower than if current inventory had been purchased and used. This overstates earnings relative to sustainable operations. ASC 330-10-50-7 requires disclosure of LIFO liquidations to alert users to these artificial profits.
explanations.c: LIFO liquidation directly reduces COGS (by using cheaper historical-cost layers) — producing a measurable income effect.
explanations.d: LIFO liquidation creates higher income (not lower) in rising-price environments.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company overstates ending inventory by $40,000 in Year 1. What is the effect on Year 1 income, Year 2 income, and two-year cumulative income?

answers.text: Year 1 income: overstated $40,000; Year 2 income: unaffected; two-year total: overstated $40,000
Year 1 income: unaffected; Year 2 income: overstated $40,000; two-year total: overstated $40,000
Year 1 income: unaffected; Year 2 income: understated $40,000; two-year total: zero net effect
Year 1 income: overstated $40,000; Year 2 income: understated $40,000; two-year total: zero — errors self-correct because Year 1 ending inventory becomes Year 2 beginning inventory

explanations.a: While Year 1 is correctly identified as overstated, Year 2 IS affected — the overstated Year 1 ending inventory becomes Year 2 beginning inventory, inflating Year 2 COGS and understating Year 2 income.
explanations.b: Year 1 income IS affected — overstatement of ending inventory understates Year 1 COGS and overstates Year 1 income.
explanations.c: Year 1 income IS affected (overstated), not unaffected.
explanations.d: Inventory errors are self-correcting over two periods: Year 1 — Ending inventory overstated $40,000 → COGS understated $40,000 → Net income overstated $40,000. Year 2 — Overstated Year 1 ending inventory becomes overstated Year 2 beginning inventory → Year 2 COGS overstated $40,000 → Year 2 net income understated $40,000. Two-year cumulative: $40,000 + (−$40,000) = $0 net. Self-correction occurs, but each year's statements are individually misstated and require retrospective correction under ASC 250 if material.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under the conventional retail inventory method, how does the treatment of net markdowns in the cost ratio differ from the average cost retail method, and what accounting effect does this produce?

answers.text: Conventional method includes net markdowns in the cost ratio denominator — producing a HIGHER cost ratio than average cost
Both methods treat markdowns identically — the only difference is how markups are handled

Conventional method EXCLUDES net markdowns from the cost ratio denominator, producing a LOWER cost ratio than average cost — this approximates the lower of average cost or market (LCM) by reducing the ending inventory cost estimate
Conventional method defers all markdowns to subsequent periods — they are not included in the current-year calculation

explanations.a: Conventional EXCLUDES markdowns from the denominator — producing a LOWER cost ratio, not higher. Excluding markdowns means fewer retail dollars relative to the same cost numerator.
explanations.b: The treatment of markdowns is the KEY difference between the two methods: average cost retail INCLUDES markdowns in the denominator; conventional EXCLUDES them. Both include markups.
explanations.c: Conventional retail method denominator = Beginning retail + Purchases + Net markups (markdowns EXCLUDED). Cost ratio = Cost numerator / Retail denominator. Markdowns ARE included when computing ending retail inventory. Applying the lower cost ratio to ending retail inventory approximates LCM — understating cost relative to what average cost would produce. The average cost method includes markdowns in the denominator, producing a higher cost ratio closer to actual average cost.
explanations.d: Markdowns are not deferred — they affect the current-year ending retail inventory calculation. Only the cost ratio denominator excludes them under the conventional method.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under dollar-value LIFO, when does a new LIFO layer arise, and how is it measured?

answers.text: A new layer is added when ending inventory in base-year dollars exceeds beginning inventory in base-year dollars — the new layer is measured by multiplying the base-year dollar increment by the current-year price index to convert it to current-year cost
A new layer is added when ending inventory in current-year dollars exceeds beginning inventory in current-year dollars — recorded at current-year cost without index conversion
A new layer is added when the unit count increases — dollar-value LIFO uses unit counts, not dollar amounts
A new layer is added every year — all inventory additions automatically create a new layer at current cost

explanations.a: Dollar-value LIFO eliminates tracking specific unit quantities by measuring changes in dollar terms adjusted for price changes. Procedure: (1) Convert ending inventory to base-year dollars by dividing by the current-year price index; (2) Compare to beginning inventory at base-year prices; (3) If ending exceeds beginning in base-year dollars, a real inventory increase occurred — add a new layer; (4) Measure the new layer: base-year dollar increment × current-year price index = current-year cost. This groups real inventory growth into annual layers priced at the cost level of the year added.
explanations.b: Dollar-value LIFO uses base-year dollars (not current-year dollars) for the comparison — this isolates real quantity changes from price changes. Using current-year dollars would not properly separate these two effects.
explanations.c: Dollar-value LIFO measures inventory in price-adjusted dollars rather than tracking specific unit quantities — this is its primary advantage over traditional unit LIFO for entities with changing product mixes.
explanations.d: A new layer is only added when real inventory growth occurs (base-year dollar increase). If inventory declines or stays constant in base-year dollars, no new layer is added — older layers may be liquidated.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under US GAAP, which costs are capitalized as part of the initial cost of purchased equipment?

answers.text: Only the purchase invoice price — all other costs are expensed
Purchase price, freight-in, installation costs, and costs to prepare the asset for intended use — but NOT ordinary repairs or maintenance after the asset is placed in service
All costs incurred during the first year of ownership, including routine maintenance and supplies
Purchase price and sales tax only — freight and installation are period expenses

explanations.a: Many costs beyond the invoice price are capitalized — including freight, installation, and preparation costs.
explanations.b: ASC 360-10-30 requires capitalizing all costs necessary to bring a long-lived asset to its intended use and location: purchase price (net of trade discounts), applicable sales taxes, freight and delivery, installation, and testing to verify proper operation. After the asset is placed in service, ordinary maintenance and repairs are expensed — only betterments extending useful life or improving capacity are capitalized.
explanations.c: Not all first-year costs are capitalized. Routine maintenance is always expensed, even in the first year.
explanations.d: Freight-in and installation costs are specifically included in capitalized PP&E cost — they are necessary to bring the asset to its intended location and condition for use.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A machine is purchased for $200,000 with a $20,000 estimated salvage value and 10-year useful life. What is the annual straight-line depreciation expense?

answers.text: $20,000 per year — $200,000 / 10 years (ignoring salvage value)
$18,000 per year — described as $200,000 / 10 with $20,000 subtracted at end

explanations.a: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) / Useful life = ($200,000 − $20,000) / 10 = $180,000 / 10 = $18,000 per year. The salvage value is subtracted from cost before dividing because the asset is expected to retain $20,000 of value — that residual is not depreciated.
explanations.b: Ignoring salvage value overstates annual depreciation. The $20,000 residual value represents expected remaining economic value and is not depreciated.
explanations.c: The proper formula subtracts salvage value from cost first, then divides — the mechanics described in this option are incorrect.
explanations.d: Adding salvage value to cost would overstate the depreciable base. Salvage value reduces (not increases) the amount to be depreciated.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A $100,000 machine has a 5-year useful life and no salvage value. Using the double-declining balance (DDB) method, what is depreciation in Year 2?

answers.text: $40,000 — DDB rate (40%) applied to original cost in Year 2
$20,000 — straight-line equivalent
$24,000 — DDB rate (40%) applied to Year 2 beginning book value of $60,000
$32,000 — DDB applied to average book value during Year 2

explanations.a: DDB in Year 2 applies the rate to beginning book value — not original cost. Original cost was the starting book value only in Year 1.
explanations.b: $20,000 is the straight-line amount — not DDB.
explanations.c: DDB rate = 2 / Useful life = 2/5 = 40%. Year 1: 40% × $100,000 = $40,000; book value at end Year 1 = $60,000. Year 2: 40% × $60,000 = $24,000; book value at end Year 2 = $36,000. DDB applies the constant 40% rate to the declining book value each year.
explanations.d: DDB is applied to the beginning book value — not to an average book value during the period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A delivery truck receives an overhaul costing $30,000 that extends its remaining useful life by 4 years and increases payload capacity by 20%. How should this expenditure be treated?

answers.text: Expensed immediately — all truck maintenance costs are expensed under conservatism
Capitalized as a betterment — the overhaul extends useful life and improves capacity, qualifying as a capital improvement increasing the asset's carrying value
Expensed over the next 12 months — interim period costs are amortized over one year
Deferred as a long-term prepaid expense and amortized over 4 years

explanations.a: Not all maintenance expenditures are expensed. ASC 360 provides specific guidance on capitalization vs. expense based on the nature of the expenditure — betterments are capitalized.
explanations.b: A betterment (capital improvement) is an expenditure that: (1) extends useful life beyond original estimate, (2) increases productive capacity or efficiency, or (3) improves output quality. This overhaul does both — extends useful life by 4 years AND increases payload by 20%. Either criterion independently justifies capitalization. The $30,000 is added to the truck's carrying value and depreciated over the revised remaining useful life.
explanations.c: Capital improvements are not expensed over 12 months as prepaid expenses — they are capitalized as part of the asset.
explanations.d: The standard treatment for betterments is to capitalize as part of the asset and depreciate over the revised remaining useful life — not as a separate long-term prepaid.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASC 360, what is the two-step impairment test for a long-lived asset group?

answers.text: Step 1: Compare fair value to book value — if fair value < book value, impairment exists; Step 2: Write down to fair value
Step 1: Compare book value to replacement cost — if replacement cost < book value, write down to replacement cost

Step 1 (Recoverability test): Compare carrying value to the sum of undiscounted future cash flows — if carrying value exceeds undiscounted cash flows, impairment is indicated; Step 2 (Measurement): Impairment loss = carrying value minus fair value
Step 1: Assess whether market capitalization has declined — if so, impairment assumed; Step 2: Write down by the market cap decline percentage

explanations.a: The recoverability test (Step 1) uses undiscounted future cash flows — not fair value. Fair value is used only in Step 2 to measure the loss amount.
explanations.b: Replacement cost is not the ASC 360 impairment standard. Fair value (typically estimated using present value of discounted future cash flows for assets without active markets) is the Step 2 measurement.
explanations.c: ASC 360-10-35 establishes the two-step model: Step 1 — Recoverability test: If carrying amount of the asset group exceeds the sum of undiscounted expected future cash flows from use and eventual disposition, impairment is indicated. Undiscounted cash flows are used (a bright-line test). Step 2 — Measurement: If Step 1 indicates impairment, loss = carrying value minus fair value. Fair value may be estimated using discounted cash flows, market prices, or comparable transactions.
explanations.d: Market capitalization decline is a potential triggering event suggesting impairment testing may be needed — but it is not the impairment test itself.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A machine originally cost $250,000 with $180,000 accumulated depreciation (book value $70,000). It is sold for $95,000 cash. What is the gain or loss on disposal?

answers.text: Loss of $155,000 — original cost ($250,000) minus sale proceeds ($95,000)
Gain of $25,000 — proceeds ($95,000) minus book value ($70,000)
Gain of $25,000 — proceeds ($95,000) exceed book value ($70,000) by $25,000; the journal entry removes cost and accumulated depreciation, records cash, and recognizes the gain
No gain or loss — the company received cash equal to fair value and the transaction is neutral

explanations.a: Gain/loss on disposal uses book value (cost minus accumulated depreciation) — not original cost. Using original cost ignores the depreciation recognized over the asset's life.
explanations.b: Both b and c arrive at the correct $25,000 gain, but option c provides the complete accounting treatment including the full journal entry.
explanations.c: Gain/loss = Proceeds − Book value = $95,000 − ($250,000 − $180,000) = $95,000 − $70,000 = $25,000 gain. Full journal entry: Debit Cash $95,000; Debit Accumulated Depreciation $180,000; Credit Machine (at cost) $250,000; Credit Gain on Disposal $25,000. The asset account is removed at cost, accumulated depreciation eliminated, cash recorded, and gain recognized.
explanations.d: The sale produces a measurable $25,000 gain that must be recognized in the income statement. Proceeds exceeding book value create a real economic gain.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A long-lived asset with a carrying value of $500,000 is classified as 'held for sale.' Its fair value is $420,000 and estimated costs to sell are $30,000. What are the accounting consequences of the held-for-sale classification?

answers.text: Asset measured at lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell: $390,000; $110,000 loss recognized; depreciation ceases; reclassified to current assets if expected to be sold within 12 months
Asset remains at $500,000 — held-for-sale classification requires only note disclosure, not remeasurement
Asset written down to fair value $420,000; $80,000 loss; depreciation continues at a reduced rate
Asset written down to $390,000 but the loss is deferred until the actual sale occurs

explanations.a: ASC 360-10-45 establishes held-for-sale requirements: (1) Measurement — at the lower of carrying value ($500,000) or fair value less costs to sell ($420,000 − $30,000 = $390,000). Since $390,000 < $500,000, a $110,000 impairment loss is recognized immediately; (2) Depreciation ceases at the moment of held-for-sale classification; (3) If expected to be sold within 12 months, the asset is reclassified from PP&E to a current asset line ('Assets held for sale').
explanations.b: Held-for-sale classification requires immediate remeasurement and reclassification — not merely note disclosure.
explanations.c: The write-down is to FV less COSTS TO SELL ($390,000) — not to fair value alone ($420,000). Selling costs reduce the net realizable amount. Depreciation also ceases (not continues) upon held-for-sale classification.
explanations.d: The loss is recognized immediately upon classification — not deferred until sale. Deferral would misrepresent the asset's current recoverable value.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A machine costs $110,000 with a $10,000 salvage value and 5-year useful life. What is depreciation in Year 1 and Year 2 using the sum-of-years'-digits (SYD) method?

answers.text: Year 1: $20,000; Year 2: $20,000 — SYD produces equal annual amounts like straight-line
Year 1: $33,333; Year 2: $26,667 — SYD allocates the depreciable base using remaining life / SYD fraction
Year 1: $44,000; Year 2: $35,200 — DDB rates applied to original cost
Year 1: $36,667; Year 2: $29,333 — SYD applied to original cost without subtracting salvage

explanations.a: SYD is an accelerated method — it does not produce equal annual amounts. Depreciation is higher in early years and declines each year.
explanations.b: SYD formula: (Remaining useful life / Sum of years' digits) × Depreciable base. Sum of years' digits (5-year): 5+4+3+2+1 = 15. Depreciable base = $110,000 − $10,000 = $100,000. Year 1: 5/15 × $100,000 = $33,333. Year 2: 4/15 × $100,000 = $26,667. Year 3: 3/15 × $100,000 = $20,000. Year 4: 2/15 × $100,000 = $13,333. Year 5: 1/15 × $100,000 = $6,667. Total = $100,000 ✓. SYD accelerates depreciation in early years.
explanations.c: $44,000 and $35,200 appear to be DDB-derived figures — not SYD.
explanations.d: Applying SYD without subtracting salvage value is incorrect. The depreciable base for SYD is Cost minus Salvage value.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASC 321, unrealized gains and losses on equity securities with readily determinable fair values are

answers.text: Recognized in net income in the period of the fair value change — all equity securities with readily determinable fair values are measured at fair value through earnings
Not recognized until the securities are sold — the cost method is used for equity investments
Reported in other comprehensive income (OCI) until the securities are sold
Deferred as a component of AOCI and reclassified to earnings when sold

explanations.a: ASC 321-10-35-1 requires that equity securities with readily determinable fair values be measured at fair value at each reporting date, with changes in fair value recognized in net income (not OCI). This is a significant change from prior GAAP, which allowed classifying equity securities as AFS with unrealized gains and losses in OCI. Under ASC 321, all mark-to-market changes flow through the income statement each period.
explanations.b: The cost method is no longer used for equity securities with readily determinable fair values. All such securities are measured at fair value.
explanations.c: ASC 321 (effective for most public entities 2018) eliminated the OCI treatment for equity securities that was previously available under ASC 320's AFS category. All equity securities with readily determinable FVs now flow through net income.
explanations.d: There is no AOCI deferral for equity securities under ASC 321. Unrealized gains and losses go directly to net income each period, not to OCI.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company holds 2,000 shares of XYZ Corp stock purchased at $40 per share. At year-end, XYZ trades at $47 per share. What is the effect on the company's income statement under ASC 321?

answers.text: Unrealized gain of $14,000 recognized in net income — ($47 − $40) × 2,000 shares = $14,000 increase in fair value reported as investment income
No income statement effect — the gain is reported in OCI until shares are sold
Dividend income of $14,000 — fair value increases are treated as constructive dividends
The shares are written up to $94,000 and the $14,000 is credited to additional paid-in capital

explanations.a: Under ASC 321, the $7 per share fair value increase ($47 − $40) on 2,000 shares produces a $14,000 unrealized gain that is recognized in net income in the current period. The investment account is marked up from $80,000 to $94,000 (2,000 × $47), and a $14,000 gain is recorded. This gain is presented as a separate line item in net income — often labeled 'Unrealized gain (loss) on equity securities.' No OCI treatment applies.
explanations.b: OCI treatment for equity securities was eliminated by ASU 2016-01 (ASC 321). All fair value changes on equity securities with readily determinable FVs flow through net income.
explanations.c: Unrealized fair value increases are not dividend income. Dividends are separate cash distributions declared and paid by the investee company.
explanations.d: Fair value changes on equity investments are never credited to APIC. APIC reflects the historical proceeds from issuing the company's own shares — it does not absorb investment fair value changes.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company holds equity securities of a private company that does not have a readily determinable fair value. Under ASC 321's measurement alternative, how is this investment measured?

answers.text: At the lower of cost or market at each reporting date — applied the same as inventory
At amortized cost — the same as held-to-maturity debt securities
At fair value through net income — the measurement alternative does not exist; all equity securities use full fair value

At cost minus impairment, plus or minus adjustments for observable price changes in orderly transactions for identical or similar investments of the same issuer (the measurement alternative under ASC 321)

explanations.a: Lower of cost or market is an inventory concept (ASC 330) — it is not applied to equity securities.
explanations.b: Amortized cost is used for held-to-maturity debt securities (ASC 320) — not for equity investments.
explanations.c: The measurement alternative does exist under ASC 321-10-35-2 — it is an optional election specifically for equity securities without readily determinable fair values.
explanations.d: ASC 321-10-35-2 provides a measurement alternative for equity securities without readily determinable fair values: the investment is measured at cost, adjusted for: (1) downward adjustments for impairment (qualitative assessment triggers); (2) upward or downward adjustments based on observable price changes in orderly transactions for identical or similar investments of the same issuer (e.g., a subsequent financing round for a private company). All impairments and observable price adjustments are recognized in net income. This alternative avoids the costly process of estimating fair value each period for private company investments.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company classifies a debt security as a trading security. During the year, the security's fair value increases by $20,000. Where is this unrealized gain reported?

answers.text: In other comprehensive income (OCI) — trading securities are marked to market through OCI
In net income — unrealized gains and losses on trading debt securities are recognized in earnings in the period they occur
Not reported until realized — trading securities use the cost method until sold
Deferred in AOCI and reclassified to earnings when the security is sold

explanations.a: Trading securities flow through net income — not OCI. OCI treatment applies to available-for-sale debt securities only.
explanations.b: Trading debt securities (ASC 320) are measured at fair value, with unrealized gains and losses recognized in net income in the period of the change. Trading classification reflects the intent to sell in the near term — therefore, all fair value changes (both unrealized and realized) flow through the income statement. The $20,000 unrealized gain is recognized in net income in the current period.
explanations.c: Trading securities are not accounted for at cost — they are marked to market each period with gains/losses through net income.
explanations.d: AOCI deferral is the treatment for AFS debt securities — not trading securities. Trading securities have no AOCI component.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company holds an available-for-sale (AFS) debt security. During the year, its fair value increases by $30,000. No impairment or sale occurred. Where is the $30,000 reported?

answers.text: In net income — AFS securities use the same treatment as trading securities
Not reported until realized — AFS securities use amortized cost on the balance sheet
As a separate component of stockholders' equity labeled 'Fair value reserve' — not in OCI
In other comprehensive income (OCI), accumulating in AOCI on the balance sheet — the unrealized gain is not recognized in net income until the security is sold or an impairment is recognized

explanations.a: AFS debt securities differ from trading securities in that their unrealized gains and losses are reported in OCI — not in net income. This is a key distinction between the two categories.
explanations.b: AFS securities are reported at fair value on the balance sheet — not at amortized cost. The fair value is the balance sheet carrying amount; it's just the change in fair value that goes to OCI rather than net income.
explanations.c: 'Fair value reserve' is not standard US GAAP terminology. The appropriate label is accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) within stockholders' equity.
explanations.d: Under ASC 320-10-45, unrealized gains and losses on AFS debt securities are excluded from net income and reported in other comprehensive income (OCI). They accumulate in accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) on the balance sheet. The $30,000 increase in fair value is reported in OCI in the current period. When the security is eventually sold, the cumulative OCI amount is 'recycled' (reclassified) from AOCI into net income as a realized gain.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company has an AFS debt security with amortized cost of $200,000 and fair value of $215,000 (unrealized gain of $15,000 in AOCI). The company reclassifies this security to the trading category. What is the immediate accounting effect of this reclassification?

answers.text: The $15,000 unrealized gain previously in AOCI is immediately recognized in net income at the reclassification date — transfers to trading recognize any previously unrecognized gains or losses through earnings
No immediate effect — the reclassification is prospective only and future gains/losses flow through earnings
The $15,000 is reversed from AOCI and credited to retained earnings — not recognized in current period income
The security is remeasured to $200,000 (amortized cost) when reclassified to trading

explanations.a: ASC 320-10-35-12 requires that when a debt security is reclassified from AFS to trading, any unrealized gain or loss in AOCI at the date of reclassification must be recognized immediately in net income (earnings). The security moves into the trading category at its fair value ($215,000), and the $15,000 that was deferred in AOCI is accelerated into current-period net income. This prevents companies from 'cherry-picking' — waiting until favorable conditions to shift securities to trading and realize the gains through earnings while holding losers in AFS.
explanations.b: The reclassification is not merely prospective for the AOCI balance — the existing unrealized gain must be released from AOCI into net income immediately.
explanations.c: Releasing AOCI to retained earnings without flowing through the income statement is not permitted. The reclassification gain must be recognized in net income.
explanations.d: When reclassified to trading, the security continues to be measured at fair value ($215,000) — not reset to amortized cost.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASC 820's fair value hierarchy, a bond that is not actively traded but whose value is estimated using observable market data such as benchmark interest rates and credit spreads for comparable issuers would be classified as

answers.text: Level 1 — all bond prices are observable in bond markets
Level 3 — any instrument not actively traded uses unobservable inputs
Level 2 — the valuation uses observable inputs other than Level 1 quoted prices (such as comparable market data, benchmark rates, and credit spreads) rather than direct quoted prices
Level 1 if the issuer is investment-grade, Level 3 if the issuer is high-yield

explanations.a: Level 1 requires quoted prices in active markets for identical assets — not similar or comparable instruments. An illiquid bond without active market quotes does not qualify for Level 1.
explanations.b: Level 3 uses unobservable inputs based on the entity's own assumptions. Using observable market data (benchmark rates, credit spreads) from comparable issuers provides corroborated market inputs — this is a Level 2 characteristic.
explanations.c: ASC 820's fair value hierarchy: Level 1 = quoted prices for identical assets in active markets (highest priority); Level 2 = observable inputs other than Level 1, including: quoted prices for similar assets in active markets; quoted prices for identical assets in markets that are not active; observable inputs such as interest rates, yield curves, and credit spreads. A bond valued using benchmark interest rates and credit spreads for comparable issuers uses corroborated, observable market inputs — Level 2. Level 3 would apply if the entity used its own internal credit model without observable market corroboration.
explanations.d: Credit quality (investment-grade vs. high-yield) does not determine the hierarchy level. The level is determined by the observability and verifiability of the inputs used in the valuation technique.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company sells an AFS debt security for $180,000. At the time of sale, the security had amortized cost of $160,000 and a cumulative unrealized gain of $20,000 in AOCI (the current fair value = $180,000). What are the effects on net income and AOCI?

answers.text: Net income: gain of $20,000 (proceeds minus fair value); AOCI: unchanged since the fair value equaled proceeds
Net income: gain of $20,000 (proceeds minus amortized cost); AOCI: $20,000 reclassified out (to zero) — the previously deferred OCI gain is recognized in earnings upon sale
Net income: no effect — AFS security gains are always reported only in OCI even when sold
Net income: gain of $20,000; AOCI: increased by $20,000 — gains accumulate in both income and OCI

explanations.a: The gain equals proceeds minus amortized cost ($180,000 − $160,000 = $20,000) — not proceeds minus current fair value. Fair value equals proceeds in this case, so the distinction is moot here, but conceptually the realized gain is always computed from amortized cost.
explanations.b: When an AFS debt security is sold, two things happen simultaneously: (1) Realized gain recognized in net income = Proceeds − Amortized cost = $180,000 − $160,000 = $20,000; (2) The cumulative $20,000 unrealized gain is reclassified from AOCI to net income (a reclassification adjustment). The AOCI balance returns to zero for this security. The $20,000 appears in net income only once — as the realized gain. The reclassification moves the same $20,000 from OCI to net income, netting to $20,000 total impact.
explanations.c: When an AFS security is sold, the cumulative gain is 'recycled' — reclassified from AOCI to net income as a realized gain. The OCI treatment applies only while the security is held.
explanations.d: The $20,000 appears only once in net income as a realized gain. AOCI decreases by $20,000 (the deferred gain is removed as it is realized). AOCI does not increase upon sale.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: To classify a debt security as held-to-maturity (HTM), which conditions must be met?

answers.text: The entity must simply intend to hold the security for more than one year
The entity's board of directors must formally vote to designate the security as HTM at acquisition
The security must be a U.S. government-issued obligation — corporate bonds cannot be classified as HTM
The entity must have both the positive intent AND the demonstrated ability to hold the security to its contractual maturity — intent alone is insufficient

explanations.a: 'More than one year' holding intent describes a long-term investment — not necessarily HTM. HTM requires intent and ability to hold specifically until the maturity date of the instrument.
explanations.b: Board designation is not the criterion for HTM classification under ASC 320. The classification is based on management's intent and ability, not a formal board vote.
explanations.c: Corporate bonds, municipal bonds, and other private debt instruments can all be classified as HTM if the entity has the intent and ability to hold them to maturity.
explanations.d: ASC 320-10-25-1 requires two conditions for HTM classification: (1) Positive intent — management affirmatively intends to hold the security until its contractual maturity date, not just for an indefinite period; (2) Ability to hold — the entity has the financial capacity and operational ability to hold the security to maturity without being forced to sell before maturity (e.g., no anticipated liquidity needs that would require selling). The two-part test prevents entities from using HTM when there is a realistic possibility of selling before maturity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company has a large HTM portfolio. It sells one HTM security early (before maturity) due to a financial hardship not permitted under ASC 320's narrow exceptions. What is the consequence for the remaining HTM portfolio?

answers.text: Only the sold security is affected — the remaining HTM securities continue as HTM
The HTM portfolio is 'tainted' — the remaining HTM securities must be reclassified to AFS or trading, and the entity may not classify securities as HTM for approximately two years
The security that was sold must be reclassified, but remaining HTM securities are unaffected
The entity must immediately record impairment losses on all remaining HTM securities

explanations.a: Selling one HTM security before maturity (outside the narrow exceptions) contaminates the entire portfolio — the remaining securities cannot stay classified as HTM.
explanations.b: Under ASC 320-10-25-4 and 25-5, selling a HTM security before maturity (other than in specifically permitted circumstances — such as when the security has deteriorated significantly in credit quality, a tax law change, a major business combination, or the security is within three months of maturity) 'taints' the HTM portfolio. The entity must: (1) reclassify the remaining HTM securities to AFS (recognizing all unrealized gains/losses in OCI); and (2) refrain from classifying any new purchases as HTM for approximately two years. This rule enforces discipline — it prevents selective selling of HTM securities while claiming intent to hold the rest.
explanations.c: Tainting affects the entire remaining portfolio, not just the sold security.
explanations.d: Tainting requires reclassification — not automatic impairment of remaining securities. Impairment is assessed separately based on credit quality.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company purchases a $1,000 face value bond for $1,050 (at a premium). The bond has a 6% stated coupon (annual) and matures in 5 years. The effective yield (market rate) at purchase is approximately 4.9%. Using the effective interest method in Year 1, what is interest income and premium amortization?

answers.text: Interest income ≈ $51.45; premium amortization ≈ $8.55; new book value ≈ $1,041.45 — interest income = beginning book value ($1,050) × effective rate (4.9%); coupon ($60) exceeds interest income, so the excess amortizes the premium
Interest income = $60; no premium amortization — coupon equals interest income for premium bonds
Interest income = $60; premium amortization = $10 straight-line per year (premium $50 / 5 years)
Interest income = $51.45; premium amortization = $10 — the effective rate applies but straight-line amortization is required

explanations.a: Effective interest method for a premium bond: Year 1 interest income = Beginning book value × Effective yield = $1,050 × 4.9% = $51.45. Cash coupon received = $1,000 × 6% = $60.00. Premium amortization = Cash received − Interest income = $60.00 − $51.45 = $8.55. New book value = $1,050.00 − $8.55 = $1,041.45. The logic: because the coupon rate (6%) exceeds the effective rate (4.9%), the investor paid a premium. The interest income recognized reflects the actual yield earned (4.9%), not the coupon rate. The excess cash received ($8.55) reduces the premium — gradually bringing the book value from $1,050 down to $1,000 at maturity.
explanations.b: For premium bonds, interest income under the effective interest method is LESS than the coupon amount. The coupon ($60) exceeds interest income ($51.45) — the difference amortizes the premium.
explanations.c: The effective interest method is required under US GAAP (straight-line is acceptable only if immaterial). Under the effective interest method, amortization is not equal each period — it changes as the book value changes.
explanations.d: Effective rate applies but the amortization amount ($8.55) follows from the effective rate calculation, not a straight-line $10 amount.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Why does US GAAP require the effective interest method (rather than straight-line) for amortizing bond premiums and discounts, and what property does the effective interest method produce?

answers.text: Because straight-line is more conservative — GAAP always prefers conservatism in interest income recognition
Because the effective interest method produces smaller initial amortization amounts — deferring income recognition

Because the effective interest method produces a constant effective yield (constant interest rate) on the changing book value each period — this matches the economics of the investment (a constant return on capital invested)
Because straight-line is not permitted under any circumstances for bonds — even when the difference is immaterial

explanations.a: Conservatism is not the primary reason for requiring the effective interest method. The requirement reflects an accurate representation of the economics of interest-bearing instruments.
explanations.b: The initial amortization amount under the effective interest method may be smaller or larger than straight-line depending on whether there is a premium or discount. The key attribute is the constant yield — not the initial amount.
explanations.c: The effective interest method recognizes a constant rate of return (yield) on the carrying amount of the investment or liability. For bonds: interest income = Beginning book value × Effective rate. As the book value changes (decreasing for premium bonds, increasing for discount bonds), the dollar amount of interest income changes each period — but the rate (yield) remains constant. This accurately reflects the economic substance: the investor earns the same yield throughout the holding period. Straight-line produces equal dollar amortization each period but a changing effective rate — less representative of economic reality.
explanations.d: Straight-line amortization is permitted under US GAAP when the results are not materially different from the effective interest method (ASC 835-30-35-2 permits straight-line when immaterial).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASU 2016-13, an AFS debt security with an amortized cost of $100,000 has declined in fair value to $88,000. Management determines that $7,000 of the $12,000 decline is attributable to credit losses (expected not to be recovered) and $5,000 is due to interest rate increases. How is the impairment recorded?

answers.text: Recognize the entire $12,000 decline in net income — all fair value decreases are impairment losses
Recognize $7,000 credit loss in OCI; recognize $5,000 interest rate component in net income
No impairment recognized — AFS securities are only impaired when the fair value is below amortized cost on the sale date

Recognize $7,000 credit loss in net income through an allowance for credit losses; recognize $5,000 non-credit (interest rate) component in OCI — the allowance is capped at the amount by which amortized cost exceeds fair value

explanations.a: Not all fair value decline is recognized in net income. ASU 2016-13 bifurcates the decline into credit and non-credit components with different accounting treatment.
explanations.b: This reverses the components — credit losses go to net income (not OCI); the non-credit component stays in OCI (not net income).
explanations.c: AFS debt security impairment is recognized when the fair value is below amortized cost and credit losses exist — it is not deferred until sale.
explanations.d: ASU 2016-13 (ASC 326-30) introduced an allowance-based model for AFS debt security impairment: (1) Credit loss component ($7,000) — recognized in net income through an allowance for credit losses. The allowance reduces the net carrying amount but does not change amortized cost; (2) Non-credit component ($5,000, related to interest rate changes) — remains in OCI; not recognized in net income. Key constraint: the allowance cannot exceed the excess of amortized cost over fair value ($12,000 ceiling). Since $7,000 < $12,000, the allowance of $7,000 is within the ceiling. This approach separates what is economically a credit impairment (income statement event) from what is a temporary market movement (OCI).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
