questions.text: A company purchases a $1,000 face value HTM bond at a discount for $920, with a 5% stated coupon (annual), 4-year maturity, and an effective yield of approximately 7.2%. Using the effective interest method in Year 1, what is interest income and the discount amortization?

answers.text: Interest income = $50; discount amortization = $0 — HTM bonds use only the coupon rate for interest income
Interest income ≈ $66.24; discount amortization ≈ $16.24 — interest income = $920 × 7.2%; coupon received = $50; discount amortization = excess of interest income over coupon
Interest income = $50; discount amortization = $20 straight-line ($80 discount / 4 years)
Interest income ≈ $66.24; discount amortization ≈ $16.24; new book value ≈ $936.24 — discount amortization increases book value toward face value

explanations.a: HTM bonds use the effective interest method — interest income = book value × effective rate. Using only the coupon rate ignores the economics of holding a discounted bond.
explanations.b: Both b and d arrive at the same interest income and amortization amounts. Option d additionally provides the new book value, which demonstrates the correct accounting effect.
explanations.c: Straight-line amortization ($20/year) would produce equal annual amortization. The effective interest method produces amortization that increases each year as the book value grows.
explanations.d: Effective interest method: Year 1 interest income = $920 × 7.2% = $66.24. Cash coupon received = $1,000 × 5% = $50.00. Discount amortization = Interest income − Coupon = $66.24 − $50.00 = $16.24. New book value = $920 + $16.24 = $936.24. The logic: the investor paid only $920 for a $1,000 bond because the 5% coupon is below the market rate (7.2%). Interest income reflects the 7.2% return on the $920 investment. The extra $16.24 above the coupon accretes the bond toward its $1,000 face value — this is the discount amortization.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under CECL (ASC 326-20), a company holds HTM corporate bonds with an amortized cost of $5,000,000. Based on historical default rates, current economic conditions, and forward-looking credit forecasts, management estimates lifetime expected credit losses of $80,000. How is this recognized?

answers.text: No recognition required — HTM securities at amortized cost are exempt from CECL because they are measured at cost, not fair value
$80,000 recognized in OCI as an unrealized loss — CECL losses on HTM bonds flow through OCI
$80,000 recognized as a credit loss expense in net income through an allowance for credit losses; the HTM securities' net carrying amount becomes $4,920,000 — CECL applies to HTM securities
$80,000 deferred in AOCI until individual bonds default or are sold

explanations.a: CECL explicitly covers HTM debt securities (ASC 326-20). HTM's amortized cost measurement does not exempt them from credit loss recognition.
explanations.b: CECL losses on HTM securities flow through net income — not OCI. OCI treatment applies to the non-credit portion of AFS security fair value changes, not to HTM credit losses.
explanations.c: ASC 326-20 requires entities to recognize an allowance for expected credit losses on HTM debt securities. The recognition is Day 1 (at origination or purchase) based on expected lifetime credit losses. The $80,000 is recognized as credit loss expense in net income and as an allowance for credit losses (contra-asset) reducing the net carrying amount of the HTM portfolio from $5,000,000 to $4,920,000. This is a significant change from pre-CECL GAAP, which did not require HTM holders to recognize an allowance until credit losses were 'incurred.'
explanations.d: CECL losses are recognized immediately in net income — not deferred in AOCI. The current-period recognition of expected losses is a fundamental feature of the CECL model.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: An AFS debt security has amortized cost of $150,000 and a cumulative AOCI balance of ($18,000) — an unrealized loss. The security is sold for $135,000 (its current fair value). What is the net income effect of the sale?

answers.text: Loss of $15,000 in net income — proceeds ($135,000) minus amortized cost ($150,000); the AOCI loss is simultaneously reclassified to net income, netting to a total loss of $15,000
No net income effect — AFS losses remain in OCI even when the security is sold
Loss of $18,000 — only the AOCI balance is reclassified; the current fair value change is not recognized
Loss of $33,000 — the amortized cost loss ($15,000) and AOCI loss ($18,000) are separately recognized

explanations.a: When an AFS debt security is sold: the realized loss = Proceeds ($135,000) − Amortized cost ($150,000) = ($15,000). Simultaneously, the cumulative AOCI loss of ($18,000) is reclassified from AOCI to net income. These amounts interact as follows: the $15,000 realized loss is the total income statement impact; the AOCI reclassification of ($18,000) reduces AOCI to zero. Net impact on net income = ($15,000) loss. Note: the ($18,000) AOCI reclassification and the ($15,000) realized loss recognition happen within the same accounting for the disposal — they net to a $15,000 loss, not $33,000. The math: when the security's fair value fell from $150,000 amortized cost to $132,000 (i.e., the $18,000 AOCI loss represents the security's fair value = $132,000), then selling at $135,000 ($3,000 above the $132,000 fair value) produces a realized gain from the AOCI baseline, netting to ($15,000) from amortized cost.
explanations.b: When an AFS security is sold, the cumulative OCI is recycled — reclassified from AOCI to net income as a realized component. OCI treatment applies only while the security is held.
explanations.c: Both the realized loss from amortized cost ($15,000) and the AOCI reclassification ($18,000) affect the income statement and AOCI, but the combined net income impact is the $15,000 loss.
explanations.d: Double-counting the $15,000 loss and the $18,000 AOCI reclassification is incorrect. The AOCI reclassification already reflects the difference between amortized cost and the prior carrying value — the net effect on net income is only the total realized loss of $15,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: The equity method of accounting for investments is generally required when

answers.text: The investor holds any shares of the investee's common stock — all ownership positions use the equity method
The investor holds 20–50% of the investee's voting stock, presuming significant influence over the investee's operating and financial policies
The investor holds more than 50% of the investee — at that point, consolidation is not required and equity method is used instead
The investor holds less than 5% of the investee — the equity method protects minority investors

explanations.a: Not all ownership positions require the equity method. Under 20% typically uses the fair value model (ASC 321); over 50% typically requires consolidation (ASC 810).
explanations.b: ASC 323-10-15-8 establishes a rebuttable presumption that an investor holding 20–50% of the investee's voting stock has the ability to exercise significant influence over the investee's operating and financial policies. Significant influence is evidenced by: representation on the board of directors, participation in policy-making, material intercompany transactions, interchange of managerial personnel, or technological dependency. The 20% threshold is a guideline — significant influence may exist at lower percentages (or not exist despite ≥20% ownership) based on qualitative factors.
explanations.c: Over 50% generally requires consolidation (ASC 810-10) — not the equity method. The equity method is not a substitute for consolidation.
explanations.d: Less than 5% ownership typically uses the fair value model under ASC 321 — not the equity method. The equity method requires a meaningful ownership stake associated with significant influence.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: An investor owns 30% of an investee. The investee reports net income of $800,000 and pays cash dividends of $200,000 during the year. What entries does the investor record, and what is the net change in the investment account?

answers.text: Investor records: Equity in earnings $240,000 (increases investment); Dividend income $60,000 (does not affect investment); net investment increase = $240,000
Investor records: Equity in earnings $240,000 (increases investment); Dividend received reduces cash and investment by $60,000; net investment increase = $180,000
Investor records: Dividend income $60,000; no entry for undistributed earnings; net investment increase = $0
Investor records: Equity in earnings $240,000 (increases investment by $240,000); Cash dividends received $60,000 (decreases investment by $60,000); net investment increase = $180,000

explanations.a: Dividends received under the equity method reduce the investment account — they are not dividend income. Treating dividends as income would double-count earnings (once when investee earns them and again when distributed).
explanations.b: Both b and d describe the correct accounting. Option d more explicitly shows the investment account changes and net effect.
explanations.c: Under the equity method, earnings are recognized as they are earned by the investee — not just when distributed as dividends. Recognizing only the dividend and ignoring undistributed earnings is the cost method, not the equity method.
explanations.d: Under the equity method (ASC 323): (1) Investee net income: Investor records Equity in Earnings = 30% × $800,000 = $240,000 (debit Investment, credit Equity in Earnings). Investment increases by $240,000; (2) Dividends received: Investor records Cash received = 30% × $200,000 = $60,000 (debit Cash, credit Investment). Investment decreases by $60,000. Dividends are treated as a return of investment — not income. Net change in investment = +$240,000 − $60,000 = +$180,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under the equity method, when the investee pays a cash dividend, the investor's journal entry is

answers.text: Debit Cash / Credit Dividend Income — dividends are recognized as investment income under the equity method
Debit Cash / Credit Investment in Investee — dividends represent a return of capital, reducing the investment account rather than creating dividend income
Debit Investment in Investee / Credit Dividend Income — the investment increases when dividends are earned
No journal entry — dividends are only recognized by the investee, not the investor

explanations.a: Under the equity method, dividends are NOT recognized as dividend income — they reduce the investment account. Recognizing dividend income would double-count earnings previously recognized through the equity in earnings entry.
explanations.b: ASC 323-10-35-13 requires that dividends received from an equity method investee be recorded as a reduction in the carrying amount of the investment: Debit Cash (or Dividends Receivable); Credit Investment in Investee. Rationale: Under the equity method, the investor already recognized its share of the investee's earnings (which include the earnings that fund the dividend). If dividends were also recognized as income, the same earnings would be counted twice. Treating the dividend as a return of capital maintains the integrity of the equity method's 'one line consolidation' concept.
explanations.c: The investment account increases when the investee reports earnings — not when dividends are paid. Dividends reduce the investment.
explanations.d: The investor absolutely records a journal entry when dividends are received — Cash is received and the investment account is reduced.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: An investor owns 25% of Investee Co., with an investment carrying value of $160,000. Investee Co. reports a net loss of $900,000. How much loss does the investor recognize, and what is the investment balance after?

answers.text: Loss recognized = $225,000 (25% × $900,000); investment balance = ($65,000) — a negative investment balance is recognized
Loss recognized = $225,000; investment balance = $0 (negative balances are not permitted unless the investor has additional commitments)

Loss recognized = $160,000 (limited to the carrying value); investment balance = $0 — loss recognition is suspended once the investment reaches zero unless the investor has guaranteed obligations or other commitments to the investee
Loss recognized = $0 — investors never recognize equity method losses

explanations.a: Investment accounts cannot be reduced below zero unless the investor has guaranteed the investee's obligations or has made advances. Negative investment balances are not recognized.
explanations.b: The maximum loss is not always $225,000 — it is limited to the investment carrying value unless additional commitments exist.
explanations.c: ASC 323-10-35-19 limits equity method loss recognition: the investor's share of investee losses (25% × $900,000 = $225,000) is recognized only to the extent of the investment balance ($160,000). After recognizing $160,000 in losses, the investment balance reaches zero. The remaining $65,000 of the investor's share is NOT recognized — recognition is suspended. If the investor has guaranteed the investee's obligations, made loans to the investee, or has other commitments, those additional exposures may be reduced by the excess losses.
explanations.d: Investors do recognize equity method losses — up to the carrying amount of the investment (plus any additional commitments).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: An investor pays $700,000 for 40% of an investee whose net book value is $1,500,000. The investor's 40% share of book value = $600,000. The $100,000 excess purchase price is entirely attributable to PP&E with a 10-year remaining useful life. What is the investor's annual equity in earnings adjustment related to this excess?

answers.text: No adjustment needed — excess purchase price goes to goodwill and is not amortized
$10,000 per year additional amortization reduces equity in earnings — the excess PP&E cost of $100,000 is amortized over 10 years
$40,000 per year additional amortization — the full $100,000 excess times the 40% ownership percentage
$100,000 immediate write-off in the year of purchase — all excess purchase price is expensed at acquisition

explanations.a: Excess purchase price attributable to PP&E is amortized — only excess attributable to goodwill is not amortized under current GAAP. The $100,000 allocated to PP&E must be amortized.
explanations.b: Under the equity method, when the purchase price exceeds the investor's share of the investee's book value, the excess is assigned to specific assets (or goodwill). The $100,000 excess attributable to PP&E represents the investor paying more than book value for its 40% share of assets with higher fair value. This excess is amortized over the PP&E's remaining useful life: $100,000 / 10 years = $10,000 per year. The amortization reduces the investor's equity in earnings by $10,000 annually and reduces the investment account. The net equity in earnings = investor's share of reported investee income minus the $10,000 amortization.
explanations.c: The $100,000 is the full excess amount — it is not multiplied again by the ownership percentage. The ownership percentage was already used in computing the $100,000 excess ($700,000 cost − $600,000 = $100,000).
explanations.d: The excess is amortized over the useful life of the underlying asset — not written off immediately at acquisition.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Investee Co. reports $500,000 net income and $80,000 of other comprehensive income (unrealized gains on AFS securities). An investor owns 30% of Investee Co. How does the investor record its share of these items?

answers.text: Equity in earnings = $174,000 (30% of $580,000 total) recognized entirely in net income
Equity in earnings = $150,000 in net income; $0 for OCI — OCI from investees is not recognized by equity method investors
Equity in earnings = $150,000 in net income only; OCI of investees is disclosed in footnotes but not recognized
Equity in earnings = $150,000 recognized in net income (30% × $500,000); investor also records $24,000 in its OCI (30% × $80,000) — the investor mirrors the investee's OCI in its own OCI

explanations.a: Combining net income and OCI into a single earnings line misclassifies OCI as net income. These are distinct components and must be reported separately.
explanations.b: ASC 323-10-35-18 requires investors to record their proportionate share of the investee's OCI — it is not ignored.
explanations.c: The investor's share of investee OCI is recognized in the investor's OCI — not merely disclosed in footnotes.
explanations.d: Under the equity method, the investor's financial statements mirror the investee's financial performance proportionately: (1) Net income component: Equity in earnings = 30% × $500,000 = $150,000 recognized in investor's net income. Investment account increases by $150,000; (2) OCI component: Investor records 30% × $80,000 = $24,000 in its own OCI (as 'Share of investee OCI'). Investment account increases by $24,000. Total investment account increase = $174,000. This approach ensures the investor's financial statements comprehensively reflect the economic performance of the investee, including both operating results and other value changes.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A 35%-owner investor sells inventory to Investee Co. (a downstream sale) for $100,000. The inventory cost was $70,000. At year-end, 40% of this inventory remains in Investee Co.'s warehouse unsold. How does the investor adjust its equity in earnings?

answers.text: No adjustment — intercompany profits are eliminated only in full consolidation, not under the equity method
Reduce equity in earnings by $30,000 — eliminate the entire profit on the transaction since it's intercompany
Reduce equity in earnings by $4,200 — 35% (investor's share) × $12,000 (unrealized profit in ending inventory = 40% × $30,000 gross profit)
Reduce equity in earnings by $12,000 — eliminate the full unrealized profit in investee's ending inventory (40% × $30,000)

explanations.a: Intercompany profit elimination is required under the equity method for unrealized profits. ASC 323-10-35-7 requires eliminating the investor's proportionate share of intercompany profit.
explanations.b: Eliminating the entire $30,000 profit would be over-elimination — it would eliminate the portion attributable to outside shareholders of the investee, which is not appropriate.
explanations.c: Downstream sale (investor → investee) — the investor eliminates its proportionate share of the unrealized intercompany profit: Gross profit on the sale = $100,000 − $70,000 = $30,000. Unrealized profit in investee's ending inventory = 40% of inventory remaining × $30,000 gross profit = $12,000. Investor eliminates its share = 35% × $12,000 = $4,200. The equity in earnings is reduced by $4,200 (and the investment account is reduced by $4,200) to defer the unrealized profit. When the investee sells the remaining inventory in a future period, the $4,200 deferral is reversed.
explanations.d: Eliminating the full $12,000 unrealized profit would attribute the entire elimination to the investor — but 65% of the investee is owned by others. The investor should only eliminate its proportionate share: 35% × $12,000 = $4,200.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: An investor applies the equity method to a 30% stake in Investee Co. (investment carrying value = $450,000). The investor then sells half of its shares, reducing ownership to 15%. At the sale date, the 15% remaining stake has a fair value of $250,000. How does the investor account for the change in accounting method?

answers.text: Discontinue equity method; carry the remaining 15% stake at its carrying value of $225,000 (half of the $450,000 equity method balance) — no gain/loss recognized on the retained shares
Discontinue equity method; the investor must retroactively restate all prior periods as if the equity method had never been used
Continue using the equity method — ownership below 20% still requires equity method if the investor was previously above 20%
No adjustment needed — the equity method and cost method produce identical results at the transition date

explanations.a: When an investor sells shares and ownership falls below the level supporting significant influence (equity method), the equity method is discontinued prospectively. The carrying value of the retained investment at the date of transition (half of $450,000 = $225,000 for the retained 15% stake) becomes the new cost basis for the investment going forward. No retroactive adjustment is made to prior periods. The retained investment is then accounted for under ASC 321 (or the measurement alternative if no readily determinable FV). Note: a gain or loss is recognized on the shares SOLD, but the retained stake is not remeasured to fair value at transition.
explanations.b: A change from the equity method to a different method is treated prospectively — not as a retroactive restatement. Retroactive restatement applies to mandatory changes in accounting principle (e.g., LIFO to FIFO), not to changes caused by a change in the investor's ownership percentage.
explanations.c: Once ownership falls below the 20% threshold (and qualitative factors confirm loss of significant influence), the equity method is discontinued. There is no grandfather provision that perpetuates the equity method for formerly higher-ownership investments.
explanations.d: The equity method and the fair value (or measurement alternative) method do not produce identical results at transition — differences in carrying values are precisely why the transition date basis becomes important.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASC 350, intangible assets with indefinite useful lives are

answers.text: Amortized over a maximum of 40 years
Amortized over their estimated useful life, tested for impairment if events indicate potential impairment
Not amortized — they are tested for impairment at least annually (or more frequently when events indicate a possible impairment)
Written off immediately — indefinite-life intangibles cannot be recognized as assets

explanations.a: The 40-year maximum amortization period was eliminated by SFAS 142 (now ASC 350). Indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized at all.
explanations.b: Amortization over estimated useful life describes finite-lived intangibles — not indefinite-lived intangibles. Indefinite-lived intangibles have no foreseeable limit to the period they contribute to cash flows.
explanations.c: ASC 350-30-35-17 requires that intangible assets with indefinite useful lives not be amortized as long as they retain that classification. Instead, they are tested for impairment at least annually by comparing the intangible's fair value to its carrying amount — if fair value is less, an impairment loss is recognized. Examples include certain trade names, broadcast licenses, and in-process R&D acquired in business combinations. If circumstances change such that the useful life is no longer indefinite, the intangible is reclassified to finite-lived and begins being amortized.
explanations.d: Indefinite-lived intangible assets are recognized on the balance sheet — they are not written off at acquisition. Writing them off immediately would misrepresent the acquiring entity's financial position after a business combination.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company acquires a customer list for $240,000 with an estimated useful life of 8 years and no residual value. What is the annual amortization, and how is it recorded?

answers.text: $30,000 per year — straight-line amortization = $240,000 / 8; recorded as Amortization Expense (debit) and Accumulated Amortization or directly reducing the intangible asset (credit)
$30,000 per year — but it is expensed directly against goodwill rather than recorded as amortization expense
No amortization — customer lists are indefinite-lived intangibles since customer relationships have no fixed end date
$24,000 per year — straight-line but over 10 years (the maximum amortization period for separately acquired intangibles)

explanations.a: Finite-lived intangible assets are amortized over their useful life (ASC 350-30-35-6). The customer list has an 8-year finite life, so: Amortization = $240,000 / 8 = $30,000 per year. The journal entry: Debit Amortization Expense $30,000; Credit Accumulated Amortization — Customer List $30,000 (or directly reduce the intangible asset account). Straight-line is the most common method, though other systematic methods are acceptable if they better reflect the pattern of consumption.
explanations.b: Amortization of finite-lived intangibles is not charged against goodwill — it is a separate operating expense. Goodwill itself is not amortized under US GAAP (ASC 350-20).
explanations.c: A customer list with an 8-year estimated useful life is a finite-lived intangible — it IS amortized. The fact that customer relationships could theoretically continue indefinitely does not prevent the recognition of a finite useful life when management has a reasonable estimate.
explanations.d: There is no 10-year maximum amortization period for separately acquired intangibles under US GAAP. The asset is amortized over its actual estimated useful life (8 years in this case).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Company A performs its annual goodwill impairment test. The reporting unit has a carrying value of $3,200,000 (including $800,000 of goodwill) and a fair value of $2,900,000. Under ASU 2017-04's simplified goodwill impairment model, what is the impairment loss?

answers.text: $0 — goodwill impairment is measured using the implied fair value of goodwill, which may be higher than carrying amount
$800,000 — all goodwill is written off since the reporting unit's fair value is below its carrying value
$300,000 — the reporting unit's carrying value ($3,200,000) minus its fair value ($2,900,000), not to exceed the carrying amount of goodwill ($800,000)
$500,000 — fair value of net identifiable assets is calculated and goodwill implied fair value is determined

explanations.a: If the reporting unit's fair value is below its carrying value, impairment exists — not zero.
explanations.b: The impairment loss is capped at the carrying amount of goodwill — it cannot exceed $800,000. Since the carrying value exceeds fair value by only $300,000, which is less than the $800,000 goodwill balance, the impairment is $300,000.
explanations.c: ASU 2017-04 simplified goodwill impairment to a one-step test: Goodwill impairment loss = Reporting unit carrying value − Reporting unit fair value = $3,200,000 − $2,900,000 = $300,000. The loss is limited to the carrying amount of goodwill ($800,000). Since $300,000 < $800,000, the entire $300,000 is recognized as a goodwill impairment loss and goodwill is reduced from $800,000 to $500,000. The old two-step model (including the complex Step 2 implied fair value calculation) was eliminated by ASU 2017-04.
explanations.d: Step 2 (calculating implied fair value of goodwill) was eliminated by ASU 2017-04. The simplified one-step approach directly compares carrying value to fair value.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under ASC 730, research and development (R&D) costs are

answers.text: Capitalized as intangible assets and amortized over their expected benefit period
Expensed as incurred — GAAP prohibits capitalizing internally incurred R&D costs because the future benefit is too uncertain at the time of expenditure
Capitalized only if management determines the R&D will lead to a commercially viable product
Capitalized if incurred after technological feasibility has been demonstrated

explanations.a: US GAAP prohibits capitalizing internally incurred R&D. Unlike IFRS (which permits development phase capitalization under certain criteria), US GAAP requires immediate expensing of R&D.
explanations.b: ASC 730-10-25-1 requires that R&D expenditures be charged to expense when incurred. The rationale: the future benefit of R&D is too uncertain — the probability that any specific project will generate economic benefits is speculative, making capitalization unreliable. Exceptions include: (1) R&D acquired in a business combination that represents an in-process R&D asset — recognized as an indefinite-lived intangible; (2) Software development costs under ASC 350-40 (internal-use) and ASC 985-20 (for sale), which have separate guidance allowing capitalization once certain criteria are met.
explanations.c: Management's belief in commercial viability is not a GAAP criterion for capitalizing R&D. Even if management is confident a project will succeed, R&D costs are expensed as incurred.
explanations.d: Capitalization after technological feasibility applies specifically to costs of developing software for external sale (ASC 985-20) — not to general R&D under ASC 730. General R&D is always expensed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company develops internal-use software. Which costs are capitalized under ASC 350-40?

answers.text: All costs from project inception through implementation — all phases of development are capitalized
Only the post-implementation costs — training and maintenance represent the primary value of the software
Costs incurred during the application development stage (coding, testing before go-live) — preliminary project stage costs and post-implementation costs are expensed
Only third-party software license fees — internally incurred software costs are always expensed

explanations.a: Not all phases produce capitalizable costs. Preliminary project stage costs are expensed, not capitalized.
explanations.b: Post-implementation costs (training, maintenance) are expensed — not capitalized. These costs maintain the software and do not create future economic value beyond the existing asset.
explanations.c: ASC 350-40 divides internal-use software development into three stages: (1) Preliminary project stage (planning, feasibility, conceptual formulation) — ALL costs EXPENSED; (2) Application development stage (detailed design, coding, testing) — costs CAPITALIZED. This is where significant economic value is created. Capitalized costs include direct labor, materials, and overhead allocable to the development; (3) Post-implementation/operation stage (training users, maintaining software) — ALL costs EXPENSED. The key boundary: costs are capitalized once management authorizes and commits to a project and it is probable the project will be completed and the software will function as intended.
explanations.d: Third-party license fees may be capitalized, but internally incurred software development costs during the application development stage ARE also capitalizable. The rule is not limited to license fees only.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: In a business combination, Company A acquires Company B. The acquisition price is $2,000,000. The fair value of Company B's identifiable net assets is $2,300,000. How is this 'bargain purchase' recognized?

answers.text: A gain of $300,000 is recognized in net income immediately — bargain purchases produce an acquisition-date gain equal to the excess of fair value of net assets over the purchase price
The identifiable net assets are written down to $2,000,000 — the purchase price determines the recorded value of acquired assets
Negative goodwill of $300,000 is recognized as a contra-intangible on the balance sheet
The $300,000 excess is deferred and amortized over 5 years as a deferred credit

explanations.a: ASC 805-30-25-2 requires the acquirer, before recognizing a bargain purchase, to reassess the identification and measurement of all acquired assets and liabilities to verify the measurements are appropriate. If the bargain purchase survives this review, the acquirer recognizes a gain in net income at the acquisition date equal to the excess of the fair value of identifiable net assets over the consideration transferred: $2,300,000 − $2,000,000 = $300,000 gain. Bargain purchases can occur in distressed sales or forced liquidations where the seller accepts below-market consideration.
explanations.b: Under ASC 805, acquired identifiable assets and liabilities are measured at fair value at the acquisition date — not written down to the purchase price. The fair values are recorded, and any excess produces a bargain purchase gain.
explanations.c: US GAAP does not use 'negative goodwill' as a balance sheet intangible. Negative goodwill was eliminated by SFAS 141 — it is now recognized as a gain.
explanations.d: Deferred credit treatment was the old accounting for negative goodwill (prior to SFAS 141). Under current ASC 805, a bargain purchase produces an immediate gain in net income — not a deferred credit.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A finite-lived intangible asset (a customer contract worth $500,000, amortizing straight-line over 10 years) has been amortized for 4 years (book value = $300,000). A triggering event suggests possible impairment. Undiscounted future cash flows are $280,000. Fair value = $240,000. What is the impairment loss?

answers.text: $0 — undiscounted cash flows ($280,000) are below book value ($300,000), so no impairment exists
$60,000 — Step 1 fails (book value $300,000 > undiscounted $280,000); Step 2 impairment = book value ($300,000) minus fair value ($240,000) = $60,000
$20,000 — the difference between book value ($300,000) and undiscounted cash flows ($280,000)
$260,000 — the full carrying amount is written off when impairment is identified

explanations.a: Step 1 requires comparing book value to undiscounted future cash flows. Since $300,000 book value > $280,000 undiscounted cash flows, Step 1 FAILS — impairment is indicated. Step 2 is then required.
explanations.b: Two-step impairment test (ASC 360): Step 1 — Recoverability: $300,000 book value vs. $280,000 undiscounted future cash flows. Since book value exceeds undiscounted cash flows, impairment is indicated. Step 2 — Measurement: Impairment loss = Book value ($300,000) − Fair value ($240,000) = $60,000. The intangible is written down to $240,000. The remaining book value is then amortized over the remaining 6-year life ($240,000 / 6 = $40,000/year). Note: undiscounted cash flows are used in Step 1 only as a recoverability test — the measurement in Step 2 uses fair value (which IS discounted).
explanations.c: The $20,000 difference between book value and undiscounted cash flows is the Step 1 test result — it is not the impairment measurement. Step 2 compares book value to fair value ($240,000), producing the $60,000 impairment.
explanations.d: Writing off the full $300,000 would be appropriate only if fair value were zero. The impairment is limited to the excess of book value over fair value ($60,000) — not a full write-off.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Company A acquires a competitor's trade name for $4,000,000 in cash. Company B internally develops an equivalent brand through $4,000,000 of advertising and promotional expenditures. How do the two companies account for these assets?

answers.text: Both companies record a $4,000,000 intangible asset — acquired and internally developed intangibles receive the same treatment
Company A expenses $4,000,000 immediately — all intangible acquisitions are expensed under US GAAP
Company B capitalizes $4,000,000 — internally developed brands are capitalizable if management can demonstrate future economic benefit

Company A capitalizes $4,000,000 as an intangible asset (and tests for impairment if indefinite-lived); Company B expenses the $4,000,000 — US GAAP prohibits recognition of internally generated brands because the cost cannot be reliably separated from general business development costs

explanations.a: US GAAP treats acquired and internally developed intangibles asymmetrically — separately acquired intangibles are capitalized; internally developed intangibles generally are not.
explanations.b: Separately acquired intangible assets are capitalized under ASC 805 and ASC 350 — they are not expensed. Only internally developed intangibles (and R&D) are typically expensed.
explanations.c: US GAAP prohibits recognition of internally generated brands. ASC 350-30-25-3 explicitly states that costs of internally developing, maintaining, or restoring intangible assets that are not separately identifiable cannot be recognized as intangible assets. Advertising and promotional costs are expensed as incurred under ASC 720-35.
explanations.d: The accounting asymmetry between acquired and internally developed intangibles creates differences in financial statements between companies that acquire vs. develop brands. Company A: $4,000,000 trade name capitalized (tested annually for impairment if indefinite-lived, or amortized if finite-lived). Company B: $4,000,000 advertising costs expensed as incurred — no intangible asset recognized. This creates a situation where Company B may appear less profitable in development years but will have lower amortization charges in future years, while Company A shows a large asset but ongoing amortization or impairment charges.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: An accrued liability is best described as

answers.text: An obligation that has been incurred but not yet paid — the expense has been recognized in the income statement but no invoice has been received or payment made
A liability for which the company has received an invoice but has not yet paid
A long-term obligation payable more than one year from the balance sheet date
A contingent liability that may or may not become an actual obligation

explanations.a: Accrued liabilities (also called accrued expenses) represent obligations that have been incurred under accrual accounting — the expense has been recognized and a liability recorded — but cash has not yet been paid and typically no invoice has been received. Common examples: wages earned by employees but not yet paid; interest on debt that has accrued but is not yet due; utilities consumed but not yet billed; property taxes that have accrued during the year. The accrual entry: Debit Expense / Credit Accrued Liability.
explanations.b: A liability with a received invoice but not yet paid is typically an accounts payable — the invoice has already been processed. Accrued liabilities arise from expenses incurred before an invoice is received.
explanations.c: Accrued liabilities are typically current — they are short-term obligations that will be settled within one year. The definition is not based on the payment timing beyond one year.
explanations.d: Accrued liabilities represent actual (not contingent) obligations. The amount is often estimated (e.g., accrued vacation pay) but the obligation itself is definite — not contingent on a future uncertain event.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: At December 31, a company's payroll records show employees have earned $85,000 in wages for December 29–31 that will be paid on January 5. What adjusting entry is required at December 31?

answers.text: Debit Wages Expense $85,000 / Credit Wages Payable $85,000 — accruing the expense and liability for wages earned but not yet paid
No entry — wages are recorded only when paid
Debit Wages Payable $85,000 / Credit Cash $85,000 — recording payment in advance
Debit Prepaid Wages $85,000 / Credit Wages Payable $85,000 — wages earned before payment are prepaid expenses

explanations.a: Accrual accounting requires matching expenses to the period they are incurred. Employees earned $85,000 during December 29–31 — this is a December expense regardless of the January 5 payment date. The adjusting entry: Debit Wages Expense $85,000 / Credit Wages Payable $85,000. This entry records the expense in December (correct period) and creates a current liability reflecting the company's obligation to pay on January 5.
explanations.b: Under accrual accounting, expenses are recognized when incurred — not when paid. The wages were earned December 29–31, so the expense and liability must be recognized in the December financial statements.
explanations.c: Cash has not been paid — debiting Wages Payable and crediting Cash at December 31 would record a payment that hasn't occurred and eliminate a liability that hasn't been settled.
explanations.d: Wages earned by employees are not prepaid expenses. Prepaid expenses are assets representing amounts paid in advance for future benefits. Wages payable are liabilities representing amounts owed to employees for past services rendered.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company sells products with a one-year warranty. Based on historical data, warranty costs average 3% of sales. Annual sales are $4,000,000. During the year, $90,000 in warranty claims were paid. What is warranty expense for the year and the ending accrued warranty liability (beginning liability = $30,000)?

answers.text: Warranty expense = $90,000; ending liability = $30,000
Warranty expense = $90,000 (only the amount paid); ending liability = $30,000 (unchanged)
Warranty expense = $120,000; ending liability = $120,000 (beginning balance ignored)

explanations.a: Under the accrual method for warranty obligations: Warranty expense = 3% × $4,000,000 = $120,000 (recognized in the period of sale to match the expense with the revenue). Accrued Warranty Liability rollforward: Beginning balance $30,000 + Accrual $120,000 − Payments $90,000 = Ending balance $60,000. Journal entries: (1) Debit Warranty Expense $120,000 / Credit Accrued Warranty Liability $120,000 (to accrue); (2) Debit Accrued Warranty Liability $90,000 / Credit Cash $90,000 (for claims paid). This approach properly matches warranty costs to the period of sale regardless of when claims are settled.
explanations.b: Warranty expense should be accrued based on estimated future costs — not limited to claims actually paid in the period. The estimated expense is 3% of sales = $120,000.
explanations.c: Recording only claims paid treats warranty accounting as cash-basis — violating the matching principle. Estimated future warranty costs must be accrued in the period of sale.
explanations.d: The beginning liability balance must be carried forward and reduced by payments. Ignoring the beginning balance produces an overstated ending liability.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A retailer collects sales tax of $18,000 from customers during November. These taxes are remitted to the state government on December 15. How should the $18,000 be classified at November 30?

answers.text: Revenue — the retailer collected the cash and it is part of gross sales
Deferred revenue — the tax is recognized as revenue when remitted to the state
Sales tax payable (current liability) — the retailer acts as a collection agent for the government; the tax belongs to the government and is owed upon remittance
Prepaid tax expense — taxes paid before the due date are prepaid assets

explanations.a: Sales taxes collected from customers are not revenue for the retailer. The retailer is acting as a tax collection agent — the tax belongs to the government, not to the company. Including it in revenue would overstate sales.
explanations.b: Deferred revenue applies when a company receives payment before delivering goods or services. Sales tax collected is not revenue — it is a pass-through obligation to the government.
explanations.c: Sales taxes collected from customers are a liability of the retailer to the government. At November 30, $18,000 has been collected but not yet remitted — it is classified as Sales Tax Payable (a current liability). When remitted on December 15: Debit Sales Tax Payable $18,000 / Credit Cash $18,000. This treatment reflects the retailer's role as an intermediary collecting taxes on behalf of the taxing authority.
explanations.d: Prepaid tax expense refers to income taxes or other taxes paid before they are due by the company itself. Sales tax collected from customers is a separate liability — not a prepaid expense of the retailer.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: On October 1, a company borrows $600,000 at 8% annual interest. The loan matures December 31 of the following year (15 months later). What interest must be accrued at December 31 of the current year?

answers.text: $48,000 — 8% × $600,000 for the full year
$12,000 — 8% × $600,000 × (3/12) for October–December
$60,000 — 8% × $600,000 × (15/12) for the full loan term

explanations.a: Interest is accrued for the period the debt was outstanding during the current year — October through December only. $48,000 represents a full year's interest, which has not yet accrued.
explanations.b: Four months would include January of next year — interest is accrued only through the balance sheet date (December 31), covering 3 months (October–December).
explanations.c: Interest accrual = Principal × Rate × Time = $600,000 × 8% × (3/12) = $600,000 × 0.08 × 0.25 = $12,000. The loan was outstanding for October, November, and December (3 months of the current year). The adjusting entry at December 31: Debit Interest Expense $12,000 / Credit Interest Payable $12,000. The remaining interest ($48,000 − $12,000 = $48,000 for next year's portion) will be accrued in the subsequent year.
explanations.d: Accruing the full 15-month interest at December 31 would recognize future periods' interest expense in the current year — violating the matching principle. Interest is accrued period by period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company has a note payable due in 14 months. The note is classified as long-term at December 31. The company's bank notifies the company on January 20 (before the financial statements are issued on February 15) that the note will not be refinanced and demands full repayment at maturity. How should the note be classified at December 31?

answers.text: Long-term — the note had 14 months remaining at December 31, so it is classified as long-term regardless of subsequent events
The note is removed from the balance sheet — liabilities that will not be refinanced are derecognized
Current — the subsequent notification (before issuance of the financial statements) indicates the note will be paid within the operating cycle; it must be reclassified to current
Long-term, with footnote disclosure of the bank's notification — subsequent events after year-end do not affect balance sheet classification

explanations.a: While the note had 14 months remaining at December 31, subsequent events before the financial statement issuance date can require reclassification. The bank's refusal to refinance is such an event.
explanations.b: The note payable is still outstanding and is a genuine obligation — it is not derecognized. It is reclassified from long-term to current.
explanations.c: ASC 470-10-45-11 requires that long-term debt be reclassified as current if, after the balance sheet date but before the financial statements are issued, the entity violates a debt covenant or the lender refuses to refinance and demands repayment within the normal operating cycle. The bank's January 20 notification — received before the February 15 issuance date — is a recognized subsequent event that eliminates the basis for long-term classification. The note must be reclassified to current on the December 31 balance sheet, reflecting that repayment will be required within the operating cycle.
explanations.d: This subsequent event is not merely a disclosure item — it requires reclassification of the debt from long-term to current. Footnote disclosure alone is insufficient when the classification itself must change.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company offers a loyalty rewards program where customers earn 1 point per dollar spent, redeemable for future discounts ($0.01 per point). During the year, customers earned 5,000,000 points. Historical redemption rate is 80%. Under ASC 606, how should the loyalty points be accounted for?

answers.text: No liability is recognized until points are actually redeemed — loyalty programs are off-balance-sheet until redemption
Recognize a liability of $50,000 (5,000,000 × $0.01) — all earned points create a liability at face value
Recognize a contract liability of $40,000 (5,000,000 × $0.01 × 80%) at the time points are earned — a portion of revenue is deferred as the loyalty points represent a separate performance obligation
Recognize the liability only when points expire — breakage is recognized at expiration

explanations.a: Under ASC 606, loyalty points represent a distinct performance obligation — a material right granted to the customer. A portion of the transaction price must be allocated to the points at the time of sale, creating a contract liability.
explanations.b: Deferring the full face value ($50,000) without considering the expected redemption rate overstates the liability. ASC 606 uses the expected redemption rate to measure the contract liability, since only 80% of points are expected to be redeemed.
explanations.c: Under ASC 606-10-55-42, customer loyalty points represent a material right — a performance obligation that must be separately recognized. The transaction price is allocated between the current sale and the points. The contract liability for points = Points earned × Redemption value × Expected redemption rate = 5,000,000 × $0.01 × 80% = $40,000. The $40,000 is deferred from current revenue and recognized when points are redeemed (or when they expire — as breakage). Only the expected-to-be-redeemed portion is deferred, reflecting the probability-weighted approach under ASC 606.
explanations.d: Under ASC 606's breakage guidance, expected breakage (points expected to expire unredeemed — 20% × $50,000 = $10,000) is recognized proportionately as redemptions occur — not only when points actually expire. Waiting for expiration would defer breakage recognition too long.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company receives a $200,000 advance payment from a customer for goods to be delivered in 18 months. At December 31, no goods have been delivered. How is this classified, and what are the financial statement effects?

answers.text: Revenue of $200,000 recognized immediately — cash receipt triggers revenue recognition
Not recorded until goods are shipped — advance payments are off-balance-sheet commitments
Long-term liability regardless of the delivery timeline — advance payments are always non-current

Deferred revenue of $200,000 (current liability if delivery is expected within 12 months; non-current if delivery is beyond 12 months) — the cash is recorded but revenue is deferred until the performance obligation is satisfied

explanations.a: Under ASC 606, revenue is recognized when (or as) performance obligations are satisfied — not when cash is received. Receiving cash before delivering goods creates a contract liability (deferred revenue), not revenue.
explanations.b: Cash is received and must be recorded immediately. The receipt of $200,000 is a real transaction — ignoring it understates assets and liabilities.
explanations.c: Classification depends on when the performance obligation will be satisfied, not a blanket rule that all advance payments are non-current. If delivery were expected within 12 months, the deferred revenue would be current.
explanations.d: When a customer pays in advance, the company records: Debit Cash $200,000 / Credit Deferred Revenue (Contract Liability) $200,000. Since the goods will be delivered in 18 months: the $200,000 is a non-current liability at the December 31 balance sheet date (delivery beyond 12 months). If delivery were expected within the next 12 months, it would be classified as current. Revenue is recognized when the goods are delivered in 18 months. ASC 606 calls this a 'contract liability' — the company's obligation to transfer goods in exchange for the advance consideration received.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: When a bond is issued at a discount, the carrying value of the bond over its life will

answers.text: Remain constant at the face value of the bond throughout the bond's life
Decrease from the issue price toward zero as the discount is amortized
Increase from the issue price toward the face value at maturity as the discount is amortized each period
Fluctuate based on market interest rates — the carrying value equals fair value each period

explanations.a: The carrying value of a discount bond does NOT remain constant at face value — it starts below face value (at the discounted issue price) and accretes upward as the discount is amortized.
explanations.b: The carrying value decreases below the issue price only for bonds issued at a premium. For discount bonds, the carrying value INCREASES each period as discount amortization adds to the book value.
explanations.c: A bond issued at a discount has an issue price below face value. The discount is amortized each period using the effective interest method: the interest expense exceeds the cash coupon paid, and the difference (discount amortization) increases the bond's carrying value. By maturity, the carrying value equals the face value — the discount has been fully amortized. This accretion from issue price to face value over the bond's life is the hallmark of discount bond accounting.
explanations.d: Bonds measured at amortized cost do not fluctuate with market interest rates. Market rate changes affect the bond's fair value — but the carrying amount under amortized cost stays on the amortization schedule regardless of market movements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company issues $5,000,000 of 6% bonds at 98 (98% of face value). The bonds mature in 10 years. What are the proceeds, the initial bond discount, and the annual straight-line discount amortization?

answers.text: Proceeds = $4,900,000; discount = $100,000; annual amortization = $10,000
Proceeds = $5,000,000; no discount since bonds are issued at face value
Proceeds = $4,900,000; discount = $100,000; annual amortization = $10,000 — straight-line spreads the discount equally over 10 years
Proceeds = $4,750,000; discount = $250,000; annual amortization = $25,000

explanations.a: Bonds issued at 98 means the issue price is 98% of face value: Proceeds = $5,000,000 × 98% = $4,900,000. Bond discount = Face value − Proceeds = $5,000,000 − $4,900,000 = $100,000. Under straight-line amortization: Annual discount amortization = $100,000 / 10 years = $10,000 per year. Each year: Debit Interest Expense $310,000 (coupon $300,000 + amortization $10,000); Credit Cash $300,000; Credit Discount on Bonds Payable $10,000. The carrying value increases from $4,900,000 to $5,000,000 over 10 years.
explanations.b: Bonds issued at 98 are issued at a discount — the proceeds ($4,900,000) are less than face value ($5,000,000).
explanations.c: Options a and c are identical in content — both correctly show proceeds = $4,900,000, discount = $100,000, and annual amortization = $10,000. Option a is the designated answer.
explanations.d: 98% of $5,000,000 = $4,900,000, not $4,750,000. A price of 95 would produce $4,750,000 proceeds and a $250,000 discount.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company issues $2,000,000 face value bonds at 104 (a premium). The bonds have a 7% coupon, mature in 5 years, and the effective interest rate is approximately 6.1%. In Year 1, using the effective interest method, what is interest expense and premium amortization?

answers.text: Interest expense = $140,000 (coupon); premium amortization = $0 — premium bonds record only the coupon as interest expense
Interest expense ≈ $126,880; premium amortization ≈ $13,120 — interest expense = $2,080,000 × 6.1%; coupon ($140,000) exceeds interest expense; difference amortizes premium
Interest expense = $126,880; premium amortization = $13,120; new carrying value ≈ $2,066,880 — the premium declines from $80,000 toward zero
Interest expense = $140,000 plus $16,000 straight-line premium amortization = $156,000 total

explanations.a: Premium bond interest expense uses the effective rate applied to book value — not just the coupon. Interest expense for premium bonds is LESS than the coupon amount.
explanations.b: Both b and c produce the same interest expense and amortization figures. Option c additionally shows the new carrying value, demonstrating the premium is declining.
explanations.c: Issue price = $2,000,000 × 104% = $2,080,000. Premium = $80,000. Year 1 effective interest: Interest expense = $2,080,000 × 6.1% = $126,880. Cash coupon = $2,000,000 × 7% = $140,000. Premium amortization = Coupon − Interest expense = $140,000 − $126,880 = $13,120. New carrying value = $2,080,000 − $13,120 = $2,066,880. The premium declines from $80,000 to $66,880. By maturity, the premium is fully amortized and carrying value equals $2,000,000 face value.
explanations.d: Adding premium amortization to the coupon gives the wrong direction — premium amortization REDUCES interest expense below the coupon level, not increases it.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company retires $3,000,000 face value of its bonds early by paying $2,850,000 cash. The bonds have unamortized premium of $60,000. What is the gain or loss on early extinguishment?

answers.text: Loss of $150,000 — face value ($3,000,000) minus cash paid ($2,850,000)
No gain or loss — early retirements are always recorded at book value
Gain of $150,000 — cash paid ($2,850,000) is $150,000 less than face value
Gain of $210,000 — carrying value ($3,060,000) minus cash paid ($2,850,000)

explanations.a: Gain/loss is computed using carrying value (book value) — not face value. The carrying value includes the unamortized premium.
explanations.b: Early extinguishments frequently produce gains or losses — they are recognized in net income in the period of retirement under ASC 470-50.
explanations.c: Using face value instead of carrying value understates the gain by the unamortized premium amount ($60,000).
explanations.d: Carrying value at retirement = Face value + Unamortized premium = $3,000,000 + $60,000 = $3,060,000. Gain = Carrying value − Cash paid = $3,060,000 − $2,850,000 = $210,000. Journal entry: Debit Bonds Payable $3,000,000; Debit Premium on Bonds Payable $60,000; Credit Cash $2,850,000; Credit Gain on Extinguishment $210,000. The gain exists because the company retired the debt for less than its book value — a favorable outcome for the company.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company issues a $1,000,000 non-interest-bearing note payable to a supplier in exchange for equipment. The note matures in 3 years. The company's incremental borrowing rate is 9%. The present value factor for $1 at 9% for 3 years is 0.7722. How is this transaction recorded?

answers.text: Debit Equipment $1,000,000; Credit Notes Payable $1,000,000 — face value is used for notes payable
Debit Equipment $1,000,000; Credit Notes Payable $772,200; Credit Discount on Notes Payable $227,800
Debit Equipment $772,200; Credit Notes Payable $772,200 — record at present value with no separate discount account
Debit Equipment $772,200; Debit Discount on Notes Payable $227,800; Credit Notes Payable $1,000,000 — the note is recorded at present value; the discount is amortized as interest expense over 3 years

explanations.a: Non-interest-bearing notes must be recorded at present value, not face value. Recording at face value overstates the equipment cost and omits interest expense over the term.
explanations.b: This reverses the equipment and discount amounts — the discount is a contra to the note payable (credit side), not the asset.
explanations.c: Omitting the face value of the note and the discount misrepresents the liability. The note payable account should show the face amount ($1,000,000) with a separate discount contra-account.
explanations.d: ASC 835-30 requires that notes without stated interest (or with below-market rates) be discounted to present value using the applicable interest rate. Present value = $1,000,000 × 0.7722 = $772,200. Journal entry: Debit Equipment $772,200 (the fair value of the asset); Debit Discount on Notes Payable $227,800 (contra-liability); Credit Notes Payable $1,000,000 (face value). Over 3 years, the $227,800 discount is amortized using the effective interest method, recognizing interest expense each year and increasing the carrying value from $772,200 to $1,000,000 at maturity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company issues $10,000,000 of 5-year bonds with a 6% coupon. Market rates are 8% at issuance. Without performing the full present value calculation, which of the following MOST accurately characterizes the relationship between the issue price, the coupon payments, and the effective interest expense?

answers.text: The bonds are issued at a premium (above $10,000,000) because the coupon rate exceeds the market rate
The bonds are issued at a discount and the coupon payments exceed interest expense — the difference amortizes the discount downward
The bonds are issued at par ($10,000,000) because the 6% coupon is close enough to 8% to be considered equivalent

The bonds are issued at a discount (below $10,000,000) because the coupon rate (6%) is below the market rate (8%); interest expense each period exceeds the coupon; the excess is discount amortization increasing carrying value toward $10,000,000

explanations.a: When coupon rate < market rate, bonds are issued at a DISCOUNT (below face value) — not a premium. Premiums arise when coupon rate > market rate.
explanations.b: For discount bonds, interest expense EXCEEDS the coupon (not the reverse). The coupon is lower than interest expense because the stated rate (6%) is below the market rate (8%). Discount amortization is the excess of interest expense over the coupon — increasing carrying value.
explanations.c: The bonds are not issued at par — a 2-percentage-point difference between coupon and market rate produces a meaningful discount. Par issuance requires the coupon rate to equal the market rate exactly.
explanations.d: When the coupon rate (6%) is below the market rate (8%), investors demand a lower price to compensate — the bonds are issued at a discount. Interest expense (book value × 8%) exceeds the cash coupon (face value × 6%) each period. The excess of interest expense over the coupon is the discount amortization, which increases the carrying value from the issue price toward the $10,000,000 face value at maturity. This is the fundamental relationship in discount bond accounting under the effective interest method.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Bonds payable with a face value of $8,000,000 and unamortized discount of $320,000 are outstanding. The bonds trade in the market at 88 ($7,040,000). For balance sheet reporting, what is the carrying value, and what is the fair value?

answers.text: Carrying value = $7,040,000 (market price); fair value = $7,680,000 (face minus discount) — carrying value equals market price
Carrying value = $7,040,000; fair value = $7,680,000 — the carrying value of debt always equals market price
Carrying value = $8,000,000 (face value); fair value = $8,000,000 — both equal face value
Carrying value = $7,680,000 (face $8,000,000 minus unamortized discount $320,000); fair value = $7,040,000 (market price at 88) — these are two different amounts serving different purposes

explanations.a: This reverses the two concepts. Carrying value = amortized cost (face minus unamortized discount); fair value = market price. These are distinct measures.
explanations.b: Carrying value of debt under US GAAP (at amortized cost) does NOT equal market price. Market price fluctuates with interest rate changes; amortized cost follows a predetermined amortization schedule.
explanations.c: Carrying value is NOT face value for discount bonds — it is face value minus the unamortized discount. Fair value also differs from face value in most market conditions.
explanations.d: Two separate measurements apply: Carrying value (amortized cost) = Face value − Unamortized discount = $8,000,000 − $320,000 = $7,680,000. This is the amount reported on the balance sheet. Fair value = Market price = $8,000,000 × 88% = $7,040,000. This is disclosed in the fair value footnote (ASC 825-10). The $640,000 difference ($7,680,000 − $7,040,000) represents the market's assessment that the bond's value is below its amortized cost, likely because market interest rates have risen since issuance, reducing the present value of the fixed cash flows.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company has $5,000,000 of bonds outstanding that mature in 13 months. The company signed a refinancing agreement with a bank in January (before the financial statements are issued) to refinance the bonds with a new 5-year loan. Under ASC 470-10, how should the $5,000,000 be classified at December 31?

answers.text: Current — the bonds mature in 13 months, which is within the operating cycle, making them current regardless of refinancing
Off-balance-sheet — refinanced debt is removed from the balance sheet until the new loan closes
Current (50%) and long-term (50%) — split based on the financing agreement terms
Long-term — the post-balance-sheet refinancing agreement with a 5-year term demonstrates the ability to refinance on a long-term basis, permitting long-term classification at December 31

explanations.a: Although the bonds mature in 13 months (technically within the operating cycle), ASC 470-10-45-14 provides an exception: debt that will be refinanced on a long-term basis may be classified as long-term if specific criteria are met.
explanations.b: Refinanced debt is not removed from the balance sheet. It is reclassified from current to long-term — the old obligation remains until the refinancing actually closes.
explanations.c: There is no provision for splitting the classification — the entire obligation is classified as either current or long-term based on the criteria.
explanations.d: ASC 470-10-45-14 permits classifying short-term debt as long-term if, after the balance sheet date but before the financial statements are issued: (1) the entity has the intent to refinance the obligation on a long-term basis; AND (2) the entity demonstrates the ability to do so — evidenced by either completing a refinancing after the balance sheet date or entering into a qualifying financing agreement. The signed refinancing agreement satisfies criterion (2) — it provides documented, contractual evidence of the ability to refinance. The $5,000,000 is appropriately classified as long-term at December 31, with disclosure of the refinancing arrangement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company violates a financial covenant in its loan agreement (minimum current ratio of 2.0; actual ratio = 1.7). The violation is discovered by the lender at December 31. The lender has not granted a waiver. How must the debt be classified?

answers.text: Long-term — covenant violations are disclosed in footnotes but do not affect balance sheet classification
Long-term with a valuation allowance — the covenant violation reduces the debt's fair value
The debt is extinguished — covenant violations cancel the obligation
Current — when a debt covenant is violated and the lender has the right to demand immediate repayment, the debt must be reclassified as current, even if the stated maturity is years away

explanations.a: Covenant violations that give the lender the right to call the debt are not merely footnote items — they require reclassification of the debt from long-term to current. Disclosure alone is insufficient.
explanations.b: Covenant violations do not create valuation allowances against debt. They trigger reclassification from long-term to current.
explanations.c: Covenant violations do not extinguish the debt — they accelerate it (potentially making it immediately due). The obligation remains outstanding.
explanations.d: ASC 470-10-45-11 requires that long-term debt be classified as current when: (1) a debt covenant has been violated; and (2) the violation gives the lender the right to demand immediate repayment (or repayment within the operating cycle). Without a waiver, the lender can call the debt at any time — making it effectively current. The debt is reclassified to current even if the stated maturity is several years away. Exception: if the lender grants a waiver before the financial statements are issued (extending beyond 12 months), the debt may remain long-term.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company negotiates a debt modification with its lender. The original debt had a carrying value of $1,000,000 and future undiscounted cash flows of $1,200,000. After modification, the future undiscounted cash flows are $1,250,000. The 10% quantitative threshold test shows the change in present value of cash flows is less than 10%. How is this modification classified and accounted for?

answers.text: Extinguishment — any modification is treated as a debt extinguishment with gain/loss recognition
Troubled debt restructuring (TDR) — modifications always qualify as TDRs if the debtor is in financial difficulty
Troubled debt restructuring (TDR) — modifications always qualify as TDRs if the debtor has financial difficulty; under ASU 2022-02, TDR accounting has been eliminated for entities adopting CECL

Modification (not extinguishment) — the change in present value of cash flows is less than 10%; no gain or loss is recognized; the new terms are applied prospectively using a revised effective interest rate

explanations.a: Not all modifications are extinguishments. The 10% test distinguishes modifications (prospective treatment) from extinguishments (gain/loss recognition). A less-than-10% change in present value is a modification, not an extinguishment.
explanations.b: Under ASU 2022-02, TDR accounting was eliminated for entities that have adopted CECL (ASC 326). For pre-CECL entities, TDR accounting applies when a creditor grants a concession to a debtor in financial difficulty. Post-CECL, all modifications are evaluated under the general modification framework.
explanations.c: This correctly notes that ASU 2022-02 eliminated TDR accounting for CECL adopters — but the question context implies a general debt modification analysis. For a less-than-10% change in present value, the modification framework applies regardless.
explanations.d: ASC 470-50 establishes the 10% test: if the present value of the modified debt's cash flows (discounted at the original effective rate) differs from the carrying value of the original debt by less than 10%, the modification is not an extinguishment. The modification is accounted for prospectively — no gain or loss; the old carrying value continues; a new effective interest rate is computed; fees paid to the lender are treated as a debt discount and amortized over the remaining term. If ≥10%, the modification is an extinguishment — the old debt is derecognized, a gain or loss is recognized, and the new debt is recorded at fair value.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: Under the criteria for a troubled debt restructuring (TDR) before ASU 2022-02, what two conditions must exist?

answers.text: (1) The debtor is publicly traded; (2) the modification involves a reduction in the principal balance
(1) The debtor is experiencing financial difficulty; (2) the creditor has granted a concession that it would not otherwise consider — reflecting the creditor's desire to maximize recovery
(1) The debt is long-term; (2) the creditor forgives at least 25% of the principal
(1) The modification reduces the interest rate; (2) the modification extends the maturity date

explanations.a: Public company status is irrelevant to TDR classification. TDR criteria relate to financial distress and creditor concessions — applicable to any entity.
explanations.b: Under legacy ASC 310-40 (pre-ASU 2022-02), a TDR occurs when both: (1) the debtor is experiencing financial difficulty — unable to meet the contractual terms of the original agreement; and (2) the creditor grants a concession — agreeing to terms (reduced interest, principal forgiveness, extended maturity, below-market rates) it would not otherwise consider, motivated by maximizing ultimate recovery rather than normal commercial objectives. Both conditions must be present simultaneously. If a modification is an arm's-length renegotiation (no financial difficulty), it is not a TDR regardless of how favorable the terms are to the debtor.
explanations.c: There is no minimum principal forgiveness percentage requirement. TDR can involve any type of concession — including only interest rate reductions or maturity extensions.
explanations.d: Any type of concession can constitute a TDR — not limited to interest rate reductions and maturity extensions. Additionally, both conditions (financial difficulty AND concession) must be present; listing only concession terms is insufficient.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company extinguishes $4,000,000 of bonds by issuing new bonds with a fair value of $3,600,000. The old bonds had a carrying value of $4,100,000 (including $100,000 unamortized premium). What is the gain or loss on extinguishment?

answers.text: Gain of $500,000 — carrying value of old bonds ($4,100,000) minus fair value of new bonds ($3,600,000)
Loss of $100,000 — face value of old bonds ($4,000,000) minus fair value of new bonds ($3,600,000) adjusted for premium
Gain of $400,000 — face value ($4,000,000) minus fair value of new consideration ($3,600,000)
No gain or loss — debt exchanges between the same parties are not extinguishments

explanations.a: Under ASC 470-50, when old debt is extinguished by issuing new debt (a substantial modification or exchange), the gain or loss = Carrying value of old debt − Fair value of new debt = $4,100,000 − $3,600,000 = $500,000 gain. The old bonds are derecognized at their carrying value (including the unamortized premium); the new bonds are recorded at their fair value ($3,600,000). The $500,000 gain is recognized in net income as a gain on extinguishment. Journal: Debit Bonds Payable $4,000,000; Debit Premium on Bonds Payable $100,000; Credit New Bonds Payable $3,600,000; Credit Gain on Extinguishment $500,000.
explanations.b: The gain/loss calculation uses the carrying value of the old debt (which includes the premium) — not the face value minus the new FV adjusted for premium.
explanations.c: Using face value ($4,000,000) instead of carrying value ($4,100,000) understates the gain by the unamortized premium amount.
explanations.d: Exchanges of debt between the same creditor and debtor can qualify as extinguishments when the modification is substantial (≥10% change in present value). The gain or loss is recognized at the time of the exchange.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company has a $2,000,000 long-term loan with covenant requiring minimum EBITDA of $500,000. At December 31, EBITDA is $480,000 — a violation. The lender signs a waiver on January 10 (before financial statement issuance on February 1), extending compliance through December 31 of the following year. How should the debt be classified at December 31?

answers.text: Current — the covenant was violated at December 31, making the debt current regardless of the subsequent waiver
