Long-term — the waiver was granted before the financial statements were issued; because the waiver period extends beyond 12 months from December 31, the loan may remain classified as long-term
The loan is written off — waivers acknowledge a default and require derecognition
Long-term with a footnote about the covenant violation — violations after balance sheet date do not affect classification

explanations.a: While a covenant violation at December 31 would normally require current reclassification, ASC 470-10-45-11 provides that if a waiver is obtained before the financial statements are issued AND the waiver period extends beyond 12 months from the balance sheet date, the debt may remain classified as long-term. The waiver obtained January 10 (before February 1 issuance) extending through December 31 next year satisfies both conditions.
explanations.b: The waiver exception under ASC 470-10-45-11: when a lender grants a waiver before the financial statements are issued that extends the compliance period beyond 12 months from the balance sheet date, the debt may remain long-term. Both conditions are met here: (1) waiver granted January 10 before February 1 issuance; (2) waiver period extends through December 31 next year — more than 12 months from December 31. The debt remains classified as long-term. Required disclosure: the nature of the covenant violation, the terms of the waiver, and any cross-default provisions.
explanations.c: Waivers do not extinguish debt. A waiver is an agreement by the lender to not exercise its acceleration rights — the underlying obligation remains.
explanations.d: The covenant violation was at December 31 — it IS a balance sheet date event. The waiver (a subsequent event) can fix the classification issue, but the violation itself was not 'after' the balance sheet date.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company repurchases its own convertible bonds on the open market for $2,200,000. The bonds had a face value of $2,000,000, unamortized discount of $80,000 (carrying value = $1,920,000), and the conversion feature's equity component was bifurcated at issuance and recorded as $150,000 in additional paid-in capital (APIC). Under ASC 470-20, what is the gain or loss on extinguishment?

answers.text: Loss of $280,000 — purchase price ($2,200,000) minus carrying value of the debt ($1,920,000)
Loss of $280,000; no effect on APIC — extinguishment affects only the income statement

The total $2,200,000 is allocated between the liability component and equity component based on their relative fair values at extinguishment; the difference between the allocated liability consideration and the debt carrying value is the gain/loss in income; the equity component is charged to APIC
Gain of $80,000 — the unamortized discount balance is reversed through net income upon extinguishment

explanations.a: Simply computing purchase price minus carrying value ignores the equity bifurcation of the convertible bond. The consideration paid must be allocated between the debt and equity components.
explanations.b: APIC is affected — the equity component of the convertible bond is settled as part of the repurchase, resulting in a charge to APIC (not the income statement).
explanations.c: Under ASC 470-20-40 (legacy convertible debt with bifurcated equity), repurchasing convertible debt requires: (1) Allocate the repurchase price ($2,200,000) between the liability and equity components based on the fair value of the liability component at repurchase (with the residual assigned to equity); (2) Income statement: recognize gain/loss = Fair value of liability component − Carrying value of debt ($1,920,000); (3) APIC: debit APIC for the equity component of the consideration paid ($2,200,000 minus the liability fair value allocated). This approach separates the settlement of the debt obligation from the settlement of the equity conversion feature — maintaining the conceptual separation established at issuance.
explanations.d: Reversing only the discount balance does not capture the full economics of the extinguishment. The discount, the equity component, and the settlement price must all be considered.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company in financial difficulty restructures $3,000,000 of debt. The lender accepts $2,600,000 in cash as full satisfaction (a TDR involving partial forgiveness). The carrying value of the debt is $3,000,000 (no unamortized discount or premium). Under legacy TDR accounting, what is recognized?

answers.text: Loss of $400,000 — the company paid less than it owed, which is always treated as a loss
Gain of $400,000 recognized in ordinary income — carrying value ($3,000,000) minus cash paid ($2,600,000)
The $400,000 forgiveness reduces retained earnings directly — not recognized in net income
No gain recognized — the forgiveness is a capital contribution from the lender

explanations.a: When a creditor accepts less than carrying value as full settlement, the debtor recognizes a GAIN (not a loss). The debtor's obligation is extinguished for less than the carrying amount — this is favorable for the debtor.
explanations.b: Under legacy TDR accounting (ASC 470-60, pre-ASU 2022-02), when a creditor accepts a cash payment less than the carrying value of the debt as full settlement: Gain on TDR = Carrying value of debt − Cash paid = $3,000,000 − $2,600,000 = $400,000. This gain is recognized in net income as a gain on restructuring. Journal: Debit Notes Payable $3,000,000; Credit Cash $2,600,000; Credit Gain on TDR $400,000. Under ASU 2022-02 (for CECL adopters), TDR accounting is eliminated and this would be analyzed under the general extinguishment framework — but the gain would still be recognized.
explanations.c: TDR gains flow through net income — not directly to retained earnings. The income statement impact is intentional to fully reflect the economic benefit to the debtor.
explanations.d: Debt forgiveness is not a capital contribution. The lender is not making an equity investment — they are accepting less than owed to maximize their recovery from a financially distressed debtor.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: In a TDR where the creditor modifies terms (extends maturity and reduces interest rate) without principal forgiveness, and the total future undiscounted cash flows under the new terms ($2,800,000) still exceed the carrying value of the debt ($2,500,000), how does the debtor account for this modification?

answers.text: Recognize a gain of $300,000 immediately — any creditor concession creates an immediate gain

No gain is recognized; no adjustment to the carrying value; a new effective interest rate is computed so that interest expense over the remaining term equates to the difference between future cash flows and carrying value — all interest going forward is computed using this new rate
The carrying value is written down to the present value of the new cash flows at the original effective rate
The modification is always an extinguishment — TDRs require derecognizing the old debt and recording new debt at fair value

explanations.a: Under legacy TDR accounting, when future undiscounted cash flows exceed the carrying value (no economic forgiveness), no gain is recognized immediately. The concession is in the form of timing relief, not economic relief.
explanations.b: Under ASC 470-60 legacy TDR treatment for a modification (no asset transfer, no equity issuance): If total future undiscounted cash flows under new terms > carrying value: NO gain is recognized. The carrying value is NOT adjusted. A new effective interest rate is calculated as the rate that equates the present value of future payments under the new terms to the current carrying value ($2,500,000). Interest expense going forward is calculated using this new (lower) effective rate, recognizing less interest expense than the original terms. The economic benefit of the concession is spread over the remaining loan term through reduced interest expense rather than recognized as an immediate gain.
explanations.c: The carrying value is not adjusted when future undiscounted cash flows exceed carrying value under the legacy TDR framework. Carrying value adjustment would occur only if total future undiscounted cash flows were LESS than carrying value.
explanations.d: Modifications under legacy TDR accounting are NOT extinguishments — they are accounted for prospectively without derecognizing the original debt.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: When a corporation issues common stock for cash at a price above par value, the journal entry is

answers.text: Debit Cash for the total proceeds; Credit Common Stock for the total proceeds — all issuance proceeds go to common stock
Debit Cash for total proceeds; Credit Common Stock for par value; Credit Additional Paid-in Capital (APIC) for the excess of proceeds over par value
Debit Common Stock for par value; Debit APIC for the excess; Credit Cash for total proceeds
Debit Cash for total proceeds; Credit Retained Earnings for total proceeds — stock issuances increase retained earnings

explanations.a: Not all proceeds go to Common Stock at par value. Common Stock is recorded only at par value; the excess above par is recorded in APIC.
explanations.b: When stock is issued above par: Debit Cash (total proceeds); Credit Common Stock (shares issued × par value); Credit Additional Paid-in Capital (proceeds − par value total). Example: 1,000 shares, $1 par, issued at $15 per share: Debit Cash $15,000; Credit Common Stock $1,000; Credit APIC $14,000. The par value system separates the legal capital (Common Stock) from the amount contributed above par (APIC). This structure protects creditors — par value represents a minimum capital cushion.
explanations.c: This reverses the debits and credits. Cash is received (debit) and equity accounts are credited — not debited.
explanations.d: Stock issuances increase paid-in capital (Common Stock + APIC) — not retained earnings. Retained earnings represents accumulated earnings less dividends declared — it does not include capital contributions from stock issuances.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company repurchases 10,000 shares of its own common stock (par $1, original issuance price $12) for $18 per share. The company uses the cost method for treasury stock. What is the journal entry?

answers.text: Debit Treasury Stock $180,000; Credit Cash $180,000 — treasury stock recorded at cost
Debit Common Stock $10,000; Debit APIC $110,000; Debit Retained Earnings $60,000; Credit Cash $180,000
Debit Treasury Stock $10,000 (par value); Credit Cash $10,000
Debit Treasury Stock $180,000; Credit Common Stock $180,000 — shares returned to authorized but unissued status

explanations.a: Under the cost method, treasury stock is recorded at the cost of repurchase — regardless of par value or original issuance price. Journal entry: Debit Treasury Stock $180,000 (10,000 × $18); Credit Cash $180,000. Treasury Stock is a contra-equity account presented as a deduction from total stockholders' equity. The cost method is the most widely used approach in practice and is simpler than the par value method.
explanations.b: This describes the par value method for treasury stock — not the cost method. Under the cost method, Common Stock and APIC are not adjusted at the time of repurchase.
explanations.c: Recording only the par value understates the treasury stock account. Under the cost method, the full repurchase price ($18 per share) is debited to Treasury Stock.
explanations.d: Treasury Stock is debited (not the cash credit). Common Stock represents shares legally issued — repurchased shares remain issued but are not outstanding. Crediting Common Stock would be incorrect under the cost method.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company reissues 5,000 shares of treasury stock (cost $18 per share = $90,000) for $22 per share ($110,000 proceeds). Under the cost method, what is the journal entry for the reissuance?

answers.text: Debit Cash $110,000; Credit Treasury Stock $110,000 — all proceeds reduce the treasury stock balance
Debit Cash $110,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000; Credit APIC from Treasury Stock $20,000 — proceeds exceeding cost are credited to APIC, not to income
Debit Cash $110,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000; Credit Gain on Reissuance $20,000 — excess above cost is a realized gain
Debit Cash $110,000; Credit Common Stock $5,000; Credit APIC $105,000 — reissuance creates new common stock

explanations.a: Not all proceeds reduce Treasury Stock — only the cost basis ($90,000) is removed. The $20,000 excess above cost is credited to APIC.
explanations.b: Under the cost method, when treasury stock is reissued above cost: Debit Cash $110,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000 (remove at cost); Credit APIC from Treasury Stock $20,000 (excess above cost). The $20,000 is not a gain on the income statement — treasury stock transactions are capital transactions between the company and its shareholders; they do not produce income statement gains or losses. APIC from Treasury Stock is a separate APIC account that tracks these transactions.
explanations.c: Gains on treasury stock reissuances are not recognized in net income under US GAAP. Treasury stock transactions are equity transactions — they affect APIC, not earnings.
explanations.d: Reissuing treasury stock does not create new common stock — the shares were already issued (just held as treasury shares). Reissuance restores them to outstanding status, recorded at cost with any excess going to APIC.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company declares a 10% stock dividend when it has 500,000 shares outstanding at $5 par value. The market price on the declaration date is $18 per share. How is the stock dividend recorded?

answers.text: Debit Retained Earnings $250,000 (50,000 shares × $5 par); Credit Common Stock $250,000
Debit Retained Earnings $900,000 (50,000 shares × $18 market price); Credit Common Stock $250,000; Credit APIC $650,000
Debit Retained Earnings $900,000; Credit Common Stock Dividend Distributable $250,000; Credit APIC $650,000 — using market price for small stock dividends
No journal entry — stock dividends do not affect total stockholders' equity

explanations.a: Small stock dividends (under 20–25%) are recorded at market price — not par value. Using only par value understates the retained earnings transfer.
explanations.b: Both b and c produce the same ultimate equity structure, but option c correctly shows the intermediate 'Common Stock Dividend Distributable' account used before actual distribution. The distributable account distinguishes between declared but undistributed stock dividends.
explanations.c: A 10% stock dividend is a 'small' stock dividend (under 20–25%). Small stock dividends are recorded at fair market value on the declaration date: Shares to be distributed = 500,000 × 10% = 50,000 shares. Debit Retained Earnings $900,000 (50,000 × $18 market price). Credit Common Stock Dividend Distributable $250,000 (50,000 × $5 par). Credit APIC $650,000 (50,000 × $13 excess of market over par). When shares are distributed: Debit Common Stock Dividend Distributable $250,000; Credit Common Stock $250,000. Total stockholders' equity is unchanged — retained earnings decrease and common stock + APIC increase by the same amount.
explanations.d: While total stockholders' equity is unchanged, individual equity accounts change — retained earnings decreases, common stock and APIC increase. Journal entries are required to reclassify these amounts.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company with 200,000 shares outstanding and a stock price of $30 per share effects a 3-for-2 stock split. What is the effect on par value per share and total par value?

answers.text: Par value per share is unchanged; total par value increases by 50% — more shares at same par
Par value per share decreases by 1/3 (to 2/3 of original); total par value is unchanged — the additional shares are offset by the lower par per share; total stockholders' equity is unchanged
Par value per share increases; total par value increases — splitting creates more value
Par value per share decreases; total par value decreases — splitting dilutes the par value

explanations.a: Par value per share adjusts proportionally in a stock split. With a 3-for-2 split, each shareholder receives 3 shares for every 2 held — the par value per share must decrease to keep the total par value constant.
explanations.b: A 3-for-2 stock split: Shares increase: 200,000 × 3/2 = 300,000 shares. Par value per share decreases proportionally: if original par was $1, new par = $1 × 2/3 = $0.67 per share. Total par value: 300,000 × $0.667 = $200,000 (unchanged from 200,000 × $1). Stock splits are not recorded as accounting entries beyond a memorandum notation — they reduce par value per share in proportion to the additional shares issued, keeping total legal capital and total stockholders' equity constant. No retained earnings transfer occurs (unlike small stock dividends).
explanations.c: Stock splits do not create value — they increase the number of shares proportionally while decreasing the price per share. Total market cap and total equity remain unchanged.
explanations.d: Total par value remains unchanged in a stock split — the reduction in par per share is exactly offset by the increase in share count.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company with 300,000 shares of treasury stock (cost method, cost $25/share = $7,500,000) retires all treasury shares. The original par value is $2 per share, and the original issuance price was $14 per share. Under the cost method for retirement, what accounts are affected and how?

answers.text: Debit Common Stock $600,000; Debit APIC $3,600,000; Debit Retained Earnings $3,300,000; Credit Treasury Stock $7,500,000
Debit Common Stock $600,000; Debit APIC $6,900,000; Credit Treasury Stock $7,500,000 — no retained earnings charge
Debit Treasury Stock $7,500,000; Credit Common Stock $600,000; Credit APIC $6,900,000
Debit Common Stock $7,500,000; Credit Treasury Stock $7,500,000 — all treasury stock retirement goes to common stock

explanations.a: When treasury stock acquired under the cost method is retired: (1) Remove Common Stock at par: 300,000 shares × $2 = $600,000 debit; (2) Remove APIC attributable to original issuance: 300,000 shares × ($14 − $2) = $3,600,000 debit; (3) The difference between treasury stock cost ($7,500,000) and the amounts removed from Common Stock ($600,000) + APIC ($3,600,000) = $3,300,000 is charged to Retained Earnings. Journal: Debit Common Stock $600,000; Debit APIC $3,600,000; Debit Retained Earnings $3,300,000; Credit Treasury Stock $7,500,000. The retained earnings charge reflects that the company paid more to retire the shares ($25) than was originally received ($14) — the excess cost is absorbed by retained earnings.
explanations.b: If APIC were sufficient to absorb the excess cost, Retained Earnings would not be charged. But here: APIC available = $3,600,000; Treasury stock cost = $7,500,000; Common stock removed = $600,000. Total debits needed in equity = $7,500,000; Common Stock + APIC = $600,000 + $3,600,000 = $4,200,000. Remaining amount = $7,500,000 − $4,200,000 = $3,300,000 charged to Retained Earnings.
explanations.c: This entry has the debit and credit reversed. Treasury Stock is a debit-balance account that is credited to remove it.
explanations.d: Treasury stock retirement involves multiple equity accounts — it cannot be settled entirely within Common Stock.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A corporation has 1,000,000 common shares outstanding, par $0.01, APIC $4,000,000, and Retained Earnings $2,500,000. The board declares a $1 per share cash dividend on December 15. What is the effect on the balance sheet at the declaration date vs. the payment date?

answers.text: Declaration date: Retained Earnings decreases $1,000,000; Dividends Payable (current liability) increases $1,000,000. Payment date: Dividends Payable decreases $1,000,000; Cash decreases $1,000,000
Declaration date: no entry — dividends are recorded only when paid. Payment date: Retained Earnings decreases $1,000,000; Cash decreases $1,000,000
Declaration date: Retained Earnings decreases $1,000,000; Common Stock decreases $1,000,000. Payment date: Dividends Payable decreases; Cash decreases
Declaration date: Dividends Expense increases $1,000,000; Dividends Payable increases $1,000,000. Payment date: Dividends Payable; Cash

explanations.a: Declaration date (December 15): Debit Retained Earnings $1,000,000; Credit Dividends Payable $1,000,000. Retained Earnings decreases; current liability created. Balance sheet total equity decreases $1,000,000 (RE down); total liabilities increase $1,000,000 (Dividends Payable). Payment date: Debit Dividends Payable $1,000,000; Credit Cash $1,000,000. Liability eliminated; cash decreases. After payment: total equity unchanged from declaration date; cash and liabilities both decrease. Key: dividends are charged to Retained Earnings (not to a Dividends Expense account on the income statement) — dividend declarations are not income statement events.
explanations.b: Under GAAP, dividends are recorded when declared — not when paid. At declaration, a legal liability arises. Waiting until payment fails to recognize this liability.
explanations.c: Cash dividends reduce Retained Earnings — not Common Stock. Common Stock represents legal capital and is not reduced by dividend declarations.
explanations.d: Dividends are NOT income statement expenses — they are distributions of earnings to shareholders recorded directly to Retained Earnings. Using 'Dividends Expense' as an income statement account is incorrect.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Select Balance Sheet Accounts
questions.text: A company reissues 3,000 shares of treasury stock (cost method; cost = $30/share = $90,000) for $22 per share ($66,000 proceeds) — below cost. APIC from Treasury Stock has a balance of $8,000. What is the journal entry?

answers.text: Debit Cash $66,000; Debit Loss on Reissuance $24,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000 — losses are recognized in net income
Debit Cash $66,000; Debit APIC from Treasury Stock $8,000; Debit Retained Earnings $16,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000 — excess absorbed by APIC first, then retained earnings
Debit Cash $66,000; Debit Retained Earnings $24,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000 — all shortfall goes to retained earnings
Debit Cash $66,000; Debit APIC $24,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000 — shortfall absorbed by APIC

explanations.a: Treasury stock transactions never produce income statement gains or losses under US GAAP — all effects are equity transactions. A loss on reissuance is not recognized in net income.
explanations.b: When treasury stock is reissued below cost under the cost method: proceeds ($66,000) < cost ($90,000); shortfall = $24,000. The shortfall is absorbed in this order: (1) First absorb against APIC from Treasury Stock (balance $8,000): exhaust this account first; (2) Remaining shortfall = $24,000 − $8,000 = $16,000 charged to Retained Earnings. Journal: Debit Cash $66,000; Debit APIC from Treasury Stock $8,000; Debit Retained Earnings $16,000; Credit Treasury Stock $90,000. Retained earnings can be reduced (but not APIC from other sources, which belongs to paid-in capital for original issuances).
explanations.c: The shortfall should first be charged to APIC from Treasury Stock before reaching Retained Earnings. The priority order is: (1) APIC from Treasury Stock; (2) then Retained Earnings if insufficient.
explanations.d: 'APIC' from the general paid-in capital pool (related to original stock issuances) cannot be debited for the treasury stock shortfall — only the specific 'APIC from Treasury Stock' account is used first. General APIC is protected capital representing original shareholder contributions.
